docs.title: Artificial Intelligence in Finance
docs.text: Welcome to the Artificial Intelligence (AI) section. This area explores machine learning and AI applications in quantitative finance, from data processing to predictive modeling. The information displayed in this section is coming from different sources such as books, articles or even certification courses I've taken like GARP-RAI.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning are transforming quantitative finance, enabling sophisticated pattern recognition, prediction, and decision-making at scale.

The term AI was coined in 1956 by John MacCarthy together with Marvin Minsky of Harvard, Nathan Rochester of IBM, and Claude Shannon of Bell. All together echoed Turing's notion 1 stating that learning-related process and other feature of intelligence can be in principle desscribed such that a machine may simulate it.

Turing Machine

The Turing Machine is an ideal, abstract computational model rather than a physical device. Conceived by Alan Turing in 19363, and it serves as a mathematical framework for understanding what computation fundamentally means. Some characteristics are:

  • Abstract Nature: A theoretical device designed to formalize the concept of computability without physical constraints
  • Simple Components: Consists of an infinite tape divided into cells, a read/write head, and a finite state control
  • Universal Principle: Capable of simulating any algorithm or computational process, establishing the foundation for modern computer science
  • Deterministic Operation: Follows precise rules based on the current state and input symbol

The Turing Machine demonstrated that complex computations could be reduced to elementary mechanical operations by reading symbols, writing symbols, and moving along a tape. This formalization proved that any algorithmic process could theoretically be executed by such a machine, a concept known as Turing Completeness.

Though never built as originally described, the Turing Machine's principles directly influenced the architecture of programmable digital computers that emerged in the following decades.

docs.title: Classical AI
docs.text:
Classical Artificial Intelligence, also called symbolic AI or Good Old-Fashioned AI (GOFAI), is an approach to building intelligent systems based on explicit rules, logic, and symbolic reasoning. Instead of learning patterns from large datasets, classical AI systems represent knowledge in structured forms such as symbols, rules, and logical statements, by means manipulating them through well-defined algorithms.

One of the most influential figures in the foundations of classical AI was Alan Turing. Although he worked before AI became an established field, Turing laid the theoretical groundwork for modern computing. However, mathematical logicians explored before Turing the solution to the question "What are the fundamental capabilities and limitations of computers?". Then, in his 1936 paper introducing the concept of the Turing machine, he formalized the idea of computation as a mechanical process, as a revolutionary idea beyond the work of other mathematitians on computability theory (See Sipser 4, chapter 0). This abstract model demonstrated that any calculation could, in principle, be performed by a sufficiently powerful machine following simple symbolic rules. This insight became fundamental to the development of programmable digital computers, which later made AI research possible.

Turing also contributed directly to philosophical and practical discussions about machine intelligence. In his 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence,” he proposed what is now known as the Turing Test. The test suggests that if a machine can engage in a conversation indistinguishable from that of a human, it could be considered intelligent. This idea shifted the debate about AI from abstract definitions of “thinking” to observable behavior, influencing generations of AI researchers.

Classical AI systems that emerged in the decades after Turing’s work—such as logic-based theorem provers and early expert systems—were built on the assumption that intelligence could be achieved through symbolic manipulation, an idea closely aligned with Turing’s vision of computation. His pioneering theories about algorithms, machine processes, and the possibility of machine intelligence provided both the conceptual and technical foundation for the classical AI movement.

Artificial General Intelligence

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), also known as strong AI, refers to a hypothetical AI system capable of understanding, learning, and applying knowledge across any intellectual domain with human-level performance. Unlike current narrow AI systems, which excel at specific tasks, AGI would possess advanced features like flexibility, adaptability, and general reasoning abilities.

Artificial General Intelligence would demonstrate several distinguishing characteristics. It would possess domain agnosticism, enabling the transfer of knowledge and skills across diverse fields without requiring task-specific retraining. Additionally, AGI systems would exhibit self-directed learning capabilities, identifying relevant information and improving performance independently. Such systems would be capable of abstract reasoning, working with concepts, analogies, and novel problems without explicit instruction. A key feature would be contextual understanding—grasping nuance, intent, and real-world implications of decisions. Finally, AGI would achieve results with energy efficiency comparable to biological intelligence, requiring computational resources on par with human cognition.

While AGI remains theoretical and is a subject of significant debate in AI research, it represents the ultimate goal of many AI researchers. Current systems, including large language models and deep learning architectures, are considered narrow AI—powerful within their domains but lacking the generalized capabilities of AGI. The timeline for achieving AGI, and whether it is fundamentally achievable, remains an open question in both academia and industry.

docs.title: Deep Blue and Symbolic Game Playing
docs.text:
Deep Blue, developed by IBM and first deployed in 1997, represents a landmark achievement in classical AI. The system famously defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating that machines could outperform humans in complex strategic domains. However, Deep Blue's approach remained fundamentally symbolic and rule-based, aligning perfectly with classical AI principles.

Deep Blue's architecture relied on explicit game rules, heuristic evaluation functions, and brute-force search algorithms. Rather than learning patterns from data, the system used hand-crafted evaluation functions based on chess principles—material value, piece positioning, and tactical patterns—all expressed as symbolic rules. The engine evaluated millions of board positions per second using minimax algorithms with alpha-beta pruning, techniques rooted in formal logic and game theory.

The symbolic nature of Deep Blue's intelligence is crucial to understand. Every evaluation was deterministic and traceable to explicit rules programmed by human experts. The system did not learn or adapt during matches; instead, it applied pre-defined knowledge and computational brute force. This exemplifies classical AI's philosophy that intelligence emerges from manipulating well-defined symbolic representations according to logical rules, without requiring the learning mechanisms that characterize modern machine learning approaches.

docs.title: Deep Learning
docs.text: Welcome to the Deep Learning section! Here we explore the mathematical foundations, algorithms, and architectures that power modern neural networks, from the backpropagation algorithm that makes training possible to advanced architectures like transformers and graph neural networks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning focused on algorithms inspired by the structure and function of the brain, known as artificial neural networks. These models consist of multiple layers that progressively extract higher-level features from raw input data. By stacking many layers, deep learning systems can model complex, non-linear relationships and achieve state of the art performance in tasks such as image recognition, natural language processing, and speech understanding. It has revolutionized artificial intelligence by enabling machines to learn hierarchical representations from data. Unlike traditional machine learning methods that rely on hand-crafted features, deep neural networks automatically discover useful representations through multiple layers of abstraction.

Deep learning owes its remarkable success to a perfect storm of innovation: clever algorithms such as backpropagation that make learning possible, oceans of data that provide endless examples to learn from, and the computational muscle of GPUs and TPUs that let us train massive models in record time. When these three forces combine, neural networks can truly shine!

GPU vs TPU vs Other Processors
  • CPU (Central Processing Unit): General-purpose processor for a wide range of tasks; less efficient for deep learning workloads.
  • GPU (Graphics Processing Unit): Highly parallel processor, excels at matrix operations; standard for deep learning training and inference.
  • TPU (Tensor Processing Unit): Google-designed chip specialized for neural network computations; offers high throughput and efficiency.
  • Other Accelerators: FPGAs and ASICs can be customized for specific AI tasks, balancing flexibility and performance.

docs.title: Why Deep Learning in Finance?
docs.text:
Deep learning has rapidly become a transformative force in the financial sector, enabling new levels of prediction, pattern recognition, and automated decision-making. In time series forecasting, deep neural networks—especially recurrent and attention-based architectures—are used to predict asset prices, volatility, and changing market regimes, often outperforming traditional statistical models. These models can capture complex temporal dependencies and nonlinearities inherent in financial data.

Portfolio optimization is another area where deep learning excels. By leveraging reinforcement learning and advanced neural architectures, financial institutions can develop adaptive trading strategies that learn directly from market data, dynamically adjusting to evolving conditions. This end-to-end approach allows for the discovery of strategies that might be missed by conventional methods.

Risk management has also benefited from deep learning, with neural networks being employed to detect anomalies, estimate tail risks, and perform stress testing. These models can process vast amounts of structured and unstructured data, identifying subtle patterns that signal emerging risks. The ability to analyze alternative data sources—such as news articles, social media, images, and satellite data—further enhances alpha generation, providing insights that were previously inaccessible.

In the realm of derivatives pricing, deep learning models are used to approximate pricing functions for complex financial instruments, especially when closed-form solutions are unavailable. This flexibility allows for more accurate and efficient valuation in markets characterized by high dimensionality and uncertainty. Additionally, deep learning is increasingly applied to market microstructure analysis, where it helps model order flow, predict price impact, and optimize trade execution, ultimately contributing to more efficient and resilient financial markets.

Unlocking the power of representation learning

docs.title: Backpropagation Methodology
docs.text:
Backpropagation is the cornerstone algorithm for training neural networks. First formalized in the 1980s and popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams 1, this elegant application of the chain rule enables efficient computation of gradients in multi-layered networks—making deep learning practically feasible.

At its core, backpropagation solves a fundamental problem: how do we efficiently compute the gradient of a loss function with respect to every weight in a network that might have millions of parameters? The answer lies in systematically propagating error signals backward through the network, reusing intermediate computations to avoid redundant calculations.

docs.title: The Learning Problem
docs.text:
Consider a neural network as a parameterized function \(f(x; \theta)\) that maps inputs \(x\) to outputs \(\hat{y}\). The parameters \(\theta\) consist of all weights and biases across all layers. Our goal is to find parameters that minimize a loss function:

\[ \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} L(y_i, f(x_i; \theta)) \label{eq:loss_function} \end{equation} \]

where:

  • \(N\) is the number of training examples
  • \(L(y, \hat{y})\) is the loss for a single prediction (e.g., mean squared error or cross-entropy)
  • \(y_i\) is the true label for input \(x_i\)

To minimize this loss using gradient descent, we need to compute:

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial L(y_i, f(x_i; \theta))}{\partial \theta} \label{eq:gradient_objective} \end{equation} \]

Backpropagation provides an efficient algorithm for computing these gradients.

docs.title: Network Architecture
docs.text:
Let's build our understanding with a multi-layer feedforward network. For layer \(l\) (where \(l = 1, 2, \ldots, L\)):

Pre-activation (weighted sum):

\[ \begin{equation} z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)} \label{eq:pre_activation} \end{equation} \]

Activation (nonlinearity):

\[ \begin{equation} a^{(l)} = g^{(l)}(z^{(l)}) \label{eq:activation} \end{equation} \]

where:

  • \(W^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times n_{l-1}}\) is the weight matrix for layer \(l\)
  • \(b^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l}\) is the bias vector
  • \(a^{(l-1)}\) is the activation from the previous layer (with \(a^{(0)} = x\) being the input)
  • \(g^{(l)}(\cdot)\) is the activation function (e.g., ReLU, sigmoid, tanh)
  • \(n_l\) is the number of neurons in layer \(l\)

The final output is \(\hat{y} = a^{(L)}\), and the loss for a single example is:

\[ \begin{equation} L = L(y, a^{(L)}) \label{eq:single_loss} \end{equation} \]

docs.title: The Forward Pass
docs.text:
Before we can propagate errors backward, we must first compute the forward pass—evaluating the network's predictions. This is straightforward:

  1. Initialize: Set \(a^{(0)} = x\) (the input)
  2. For each layer \(l = 1, 2, \ldots, L\):
  3. Compute \(z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\)
  4. Compute \(a^{(l)} = g^{(l)}(z^{(l)})\)
  5. Output: \(\hat{y} = a^{(L)}\)
  6. Compute loss: \(L = L(y, \hat{y})\)

During this pass, we store all intermediate values \(z^{(l)}\) and \(a^{(l)}\)—they'll be crucial for the backward pass.

docs.title: The Backward Pass: Deriving Backpropagation
docs.text: Now comes the elegant part. We want to compute \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}}\) and \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(l)}}\) for every layer \(l\). The key insight is to work backward from the output layer, computing and caching intermediate gradients.

docs.title: Output Layer Error
docs.text:
For the final layer \(L\), we start by computing how the loss changes with respect to the pre-activation:

\[ \begin{equation} \delta^{(L)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(L)}} \label{eq:output_delta} \end{equation} \]

By the chain rule:

\[ \begin{equation} \delta^{(L)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(L)}} \odot \frac{\partial a^{(L)}}{\partial z^{(L)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(L)}} \odot g'^{(L)}(z^{(L)}) \label{eq:output_delta_chain} \end{equation} \]

where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication (Hadamard product), and \(g'^{(L)}\) is the derivative of the activation function.

For common loss-activation combinations, this simplifies nicely:

Mean Squared Error with linear output:

\[ \begin{equation} \delta^{(L)} = a^{(L)} - y \label{eq:mse_delta} \end{equation} \]

Cross-entropy with softmax output:

\[ \begin{equation} \delta^{(L)} = a^{(L)} - y \label{eq:softmax_delta} \end{equation} \]

(where \(y\) is a one-hot encoded vector)

docs.title: Hidden Layer Errors
docs.text:
For hidden layers (\(l < L\)), we propagate the error backward using the chain rule. The error at layer \(l\) depends on the error at layer \(l+1\):

\[ \begin{equation} \delta^{(l)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(l)}} \label{eq:hidden_delta_definition} \end{equation} \]

Since \(z^{(l)}\) affects the loss through \(a^{(l)}\), which in turn affects \(z^{(l+1)}\):

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(l)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(l+1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{(l+1)}}{\partial a^{(l)}} \cdot \frac{\partial a^{(l)}}{\partial z^{(l)}} \label{eq:chain_rule_layers} \end{equation} \]

From equation \(\ref{eq:pre_activation}\), we know \(z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} a^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}\), so:

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial z^{(l+1)}}{\partial a^{(l)}} = W^{(l+1)} \label{eq:dz_da} \end{equation} \]

And from equation \(\ref{eq:activation}\):

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial a^{(l)}}{\partial z^{(l)}} = g'^{(l)}(z^{(l)}) \label{eq:da_dz} \end{equation} \]

Combining these, we get the backpropagation equation for hidden layers:

\[ \begin{equation} \delta^{(l)} = (W^{(l+1)})^T \delta^{(l+1)} \odot g'^{(l)}(z^{(l)}) \label{eq:backprop_recursion} \end{equation} \]

This is the heart of backpropagation: errors from layer \(l+1\) are propagated backward through the weights, modulated by the derivative of the activation function.

docs.title: Gradients with Respect to Parameters
docs.text:
Once we have \(\delta^{(l)}\) for each layer, computing the gradients is straightforward:

Gradient with respect to weights:

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T \label{eq:weight_gradient} \end{equation} \]

Gradient with respect to biases:

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} \label{eq:bias_gradient} \end{equation} \]

These formulas come directly from the chain rule applied to equations \(\ref{eq:pre_activation}\) and \(\ref{eq:activation}\).

docs.title: The Complete Backpropagation Algorithm
docs.text: Putting it all together, here's the full algorithm for a single training example:

docs.title: Algorithm: Backpropagation
docs.text:
Input: Training example \((x, y)\), network parameters \(\{W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}\}_{l=1}^L\)

Output: Gradients \(\{\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(l)}}\}_{l=1}^L\)

Forward Pass:

  1. Set \(a^{(0)} = x\)
  2. For \(l = 1\) to \(L\):
  3. \(z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\)
  4. \(a^{(l)} = g^{(l)}(z^{(l)})\)
  5. Compute loss: \(L = L(y, a^{(L)})\)

Backward Pass:

  1. Compute output error: \(\delta^{(L)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(L)}} \odot g'^{(L)}(z^{(L)})\)
  2. For \(l = L-1\) down to \(1\):
  3. \(\delta^{(l)} = (W^{(l+1)})^T \delta^{(l+1)} \odot g'^{(l)}(z^{(l)})\)
  4. For \(l = 1\) to \(L\):
  5. \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T\)
  6. \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)}\)

docs.title: Computational Efficiency
docs.text:
Backpropagation is remarkably efficient. Without it, computing gradients naively would require \(O(W^2)\) operations, where \(W\) is the total number of weights. Backpropagation reduces this to \(O(W)\) by reusing intermediate computations.

Key insight: Each intermediate gradient is computed exactly once and reused across all subsequent calculations. This is dynamic programming applied to differentiation.

For a network with \(L\) layers and \(n\) neurons per layer:

  • Forward pass: \(O(Ln^2)\) operations
  • Backward pass: \(O(Ln^2)\) operations
  • Total: \(O(Ln^2)\) — the same order as the forward pass!

docs.title: A Detailed Example: Two-Layer Network
docs.text:
Let's work through a concrete example with a two-layer network (one hidden layer).

Architecture:

  • Input layer: 2 neurons (\(x \in \mathbb{R}^2\))
  • Hidden layer: 3 neurons with sigmoid activation
  • Output layer: 1 neuron with sigmoid activation
  • Loss: Mean squared error

Training example: \(x = [0.5, 1.0]^T\), \(y = 0.8\)

Initial weights and biases (randomly chosen for illustration):

\[ W^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & 0.4 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.5 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 \\ 0.2 \\ 0.3 \end{bmatrix} \] \[ W^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 & 0.8 & 0.9 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b^{(2)} = [0.4] \]

docs.title: Backward Pass
docs.text:
Output layer error (\(\delta^{(2)}\)):

For MSE loss and sigmoid activation:

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(2)}} = -(y - a^{(2)}) = -(0.8 - 0.836) = 0.036 \] \[ \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z)) = 0.836 \times (1 - 0.836) = 0.137 \] \[ \delta^{(2)} = 0.036 \times 0.137 = 0.00494 \]

Hidden layer error (\(\delta^{(1)}\)):

\[ \delta^{(1)} = (W^{(2)})^T \delta^{(2)} \odot \sigma'(z^{(1)}) \] \[ (W^{(2)})^T \delta^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 \\ 0.8 \\ 0.9 \end{bmatrix} \times 0.00494 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.00346 \\ 0.00395 \\ 0.00445 \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \sigma'(z^{(1)}) = a^{(1)} \odot (1 - a^{(1)}) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.232 \\ 0.232 \\ 0.183 \end{bmatrix} \] \[ \delta^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.00346 \\ 0.00395 \\ 0.00445 \end{bmatrix} \odot \begin{bmatrix} 0.232 \\ 0.232 \\ 0.183 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.000803 \\ 0.000917 \\ 0.000814 \end{bmatrix} \]

Gradients:

For \(W^{(2)}\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(2)}} &= \delta^{(2)} (a^{(1)})^T \\ &= 0.00494 \times \begin{bmatrix} 0.634 & 0.634 & 0.759 \end{bmatrix} \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.00313 & 0.00313 & 0.00375 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} \]

For \(b^{(2)}\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)} = 0.00494 \]

For \(W^{(1)}\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)} (a^{(0)})^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0.000803 \\ 0.000917 \\ 0.000814 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 1.0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.000402 & 0.000803 \\ 0.000459 & 0.000917 \\ 0.000407 & 0.000814 \end{bmatrix} \]

For \(b^{(1)}\):

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(1)}} = \delta^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.000803 \\ 0.000917 \\ 0.000814 \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Python Implementation
docs.text:
Here's a clean, vectorized implementation of backpropagation:

import numpy as np

class NeuralNetwork:
    """
    A simple feedforward neural network with backpropagation.
    """

    def __init__(self, layer_sizes, activation='relu'):
        """
        Initialize network with random weights.

        Parameters:
        - layer_sizes: list of layer sizes [input_size, hidden1, hidden2, ..., output_size]
        - activation: 'relu', 'sigmoid', or 'tanh'
        """
        self.layer_sizes = layer_sizes
        self.num_layers = len(layer_sizes)
        self.activation_name = activation

        # Initialize weights and biases with He initialization for ReLU
        self.weights = []
        self.biases = []

        for i in range(1, self.num_layers):
            # He initialization: good for ReLU
            w = np.random.randn(layer_sizes[i], layer_sizes[i-1]) * np.sqrt(2.0 / layer_sizes[i-1])
            b = np.zeros((layer_sizes[i], 1))

            self.weights.append(w)
            self.biases.append(b)

    def activation(self, z):
        """Apply activation function."""
        if self.activation_name == 'relu':
            return np.maximum(0, z)
        elif self.activation_name == 'sigmoid':
            return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -500, 500)))
        elif self.activation_name == 'tanh':
            return np.tanh(z)

    def activation_derivative(self, z):
        """Compute derivative of activation function."""
        if self.activation_name == 'relu':
            return (z > 0).astype(float)
        elif self.activation_name == 'sigmoid':
            s = self.activation(z)
            return s * (1 - s)
        elif self.activation_name == 'tanh':
            return 1 - np.tanh(z)**2

    def forward(self, x):
        """
        Forward pass through the network.

        Parameters:
        - x: input vector of shape (input_size, 1)

        Returns:
        - activations: list of activations for each layer
        - z_values: list of pre-activation values for each layer
        """
        activations = [x]
        z_values = []

        a = x
        for i in range(self.num_layers - 1):
            z = self.weights[i] @ a + self.biases[i]
            z_values.append(z)

            # Use linear activation for output layer, activation function for hidden layers
            if i == self.num_layers - 2:  # Output layer
                a = z  # Linear output for regression
            else:
                a = self.activation(z)

            activations.append(a)

        return activations, z_values

    def backward(self, x, y, activations, z_values):
        """
        Backward pass: compute gradients using backpropagation.

        Parameters:
        - x: input vector
        - y: true output
        - activations: list from forward pass
        - z_values: list from forward pass

        Returns:
        - weight_gradients: list of gradients for weights
        - bias_gradients: list of gradients for biases
        """
        weight_gradients = [None] * (self.num_layers - 1)
        bias_gradients = [None] * (self.num_layers - 1)

        # Output layer error (assuming MSE loss and linear output)
        delta = activations[-1] - y

        # Backpropagate through layers
        for l in range(self.num_layers - 2, -1, -1):
            # Compute gradients for this layer
            weight_gradients[l] = delta @ activations[l].T
            bias_gradients[l] = delta

            # Propagate error to previous layer (if not input layer)
            if l > 0:
                delta = (self.weights[l].T @ delta) * self.activation_derivative(z_values[l-1])

        return weight_gradients, bias_gradients

    def train_step(self, x, y, learning_rate=0.01):
        """
        Perform one training step: forward pass, backward pass, update weights.

        Parameters:
        - x: input vector (column vector)
        - y: true output (scalar or column vector)
        - learning_rate: step size for gradient descent

        Returns:
        - loss: mean squared error for this example
        """
        # Ensure inputs are column vectors
        x = x.reshape(-1, 1)
        y = np.array(y).reshape(-1, 1)

        # Forward pass
        activations, z_values = self.forward(x)

        # Compute loss (MSE)
        loss = 0.5 * np.sum((activations[-1] - y)**2)

        # Backward pass
        weight_grads, bias_grads = self.backward(x, y, activations, z_values)

        # Update weights and biases
        for i in range(self.num_layers - 1):
            self.weights[i] -= learning_rate * weight_grads[i]
            self.biases[i] -= learning_rate * bias_grads[i]

        return loss

    def predict(self, x):
        """Make a prediction for input x."""
        x = x.reshape(-1, 1)
        activations, _ = self.forward(x)
        return activations[-1]


# Example: Train on XOR problem
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # XOR dataset
    X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]).T  # Shape: (2, 4)
    y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]]).T              # Shape: (1, 4)

    # Create network: 2 inputs, 4 hidden neurons, 1 output
    nn = NeuralNetwork([2, 4, 1], activation='sigmoid')

    # Training loop
    epochs = 5000
    print("Training on XOR problem...")
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        total_loss = 0
        for i in range(4):
            x_i = X[:, i:i+1]
            y_i = y[:, i:i+1]
            loss = nn.train_step(x_i, y_i, learning_rate=0.5)
            total_loss += loss

        if epoch % 1000 == 0:
            print(f"Epoch {epoch:4d}, Loss: {total_loss:.6f}")

    # Test predictions
    print("\nPredictions after training:")
    for i in range(4):
        x_i = X[:, i]
        pred = nn.predict(x_i)
        print(f"Input: {x_i}, True: {y[0, i]:.1f}, Predicted: {pred[0, 0]:.4f}")

Output:

Training on XOR problem...

Epoch 1000, Loss: 0.006891
Epoch 2000, Loss: 0.002456
Epoch 3000, Loss: 0.001339
Epoch 4000, Loss: 0.000889

docs.title: Common Activation Functions and Their Derivatives
docs.text:
Backpropagation requires computing \(g'(z)\) for each activation function. Here are the most common ones:

Activation Function Definition Derivative ReLU \(g(z) = \max(0, z)\) \(g'(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & z > 0 \\ 0 & z \leq 0 \end{cases}\) Sigmoid \(g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) \(g'(z) = g(z)(1 - g(z))\) Tanh \(g(z) = \tanh(z) = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}}\) \(g'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)\) Leaky ReLU \(g(z) = \max(\alpha z, z)\) where \(\alpha \approx 0.01\) \(g'(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & z > 0 \\ \alpha & z \leq 0 \end{cases}\) Softmax \(g(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}\) \(\frac{\partial g(z)_i}{\partial z_j} = g(z)_i(\delta_{ij} - g(z)_j)\)

Common use cases:

  • ReLU / Leaky ReLU: Default choice for hidden layers; fast computation, mitigates vanishing gradients
  • Sigmoid / Tanh: Legacy activations; useful for bounded outputs or gates in LSTMs
  • Softmax: Multi-class classification outputs; produces probability distributions

docs.title: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
docs.text:
One challenge in training deep networks is that gradients can either vanish or explode as they propagate backward through many layers.

Vanishing gradients: When using sigmoid or tanh activations, the derivatives are bounded by 1. As we multiply many such terms in equation \(\ref{eq:backprop_recursion}\), the gradient can shrink exponentially:

\[ \begin{equation} \|\delta^{(1)}\| \approx \|\delta^{(L)}\| \prod_{l=2}^{L} \|W^{(l)}\| \|g'^{(l)}\| \label{eq:vanishing_gradient} \end{equation} \]

If \(\|g'^{(l)}\| < 1\) and \(\|W^{(l)}\| < 1\), early layers receive tiny gradients and learn very slowly.

Solutions: - Use ReLU activations (derivative is either 0 or 1) - Proper weight initialization (He, Xavier) - Batch normalization - Residual connections (skip connections) - LSTM/GRU for recurrent networks

Exploding gradients: The opposite problem occurs when gradients grow exponentially. This is more common in recurrent networks.

Solutions: - Gradient clipping - Careful weight initialization - Lower learning rates

docs.title: Matrix Calculus Perspective
docs.text:
Backpropagation can be elegantly expressed using matrix calculus. The key is to track how the loss changes as we perturb each parameter.

For a scalar loss \(L\) and matrix parameter \(W\), the gradient is:

\[ \begin{equation} \left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}\right]_{ij} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{ij}} \label{eq:matrix_grad} \end{equation} \]

Using the chain rule systematically:

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(l)}} \frac{\partial z^{(l)}}{\partial W^{(l)}} \label{eq:chain_weight} \end{equation} \]

Since \(z^{(l)} = W^{(l)} a^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}\):

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\partial z^{(l)}}{\partial W^{(l)}} \text{ is such that } \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T \label{eq:weight_grad_derivation} \end{equation} \]

This perspective generalizes naturally to convolutional layers, recurrent layers, and other architectures.

docs.title: Computational Graph View
docs.text:
Modern deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) represent computations as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Each node is an operation, and edges represent data flow.

Forward pass: Traverse the graph from inputs to outputs, computing values Backward pass: Traverse in reverse, applying the chain rule at each node

This abstraction enables:

  • Automatic differentiation (autograd)
  • Dynamic computation graphs
  • Easy implementation of complex architectures
  • Efficient GPU parallelization

The backpropagation algorithm we've described is exactly what these frameworks implement automatically when you call .backward() or tape.gradient().

docs.title: Practical Considerations
docs.text:
Mini-batch gradient descent: Instead of computing gradients for one example, we typically average over a mini-batch:

\[ \begin{equation} \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} \approx \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \nabla_\theta L(y_i, f(x_i; \theta)) \label{eq:minibatch_gradient} \end{equation} \]

This provides: - Better gradient estimates (reduced variance) - Efficient vectorized computation - Regularization effect from noise

Learning rate scheduling: Start with larger learning rates and decay over time: - Step decay: reduce by factor every \(N\) epochs - Exponential decay: \(\eta_t = \eta_0 e^{-kt}\) - Cosine annealing: smooth decay following cosine curve

Momentum and adaptive methods: Modern optimizers extend basic gradient descent: - Momentum: Accumulate gradients over time to smooth updates - Adam: Adaptive learning rates per parameter based on gradient moments - RMSprop: Scale learning rates by running average of gradient magnitudes

Regularization: Prevent overfitting by adding penalties: - L2 regularization (weight decay): Add \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|^2\) to loss - Dropout: Randomly zero out neurons during training - Batch normalization: Normalize activations within each mini-batch

docs.title: Historical Context and Impact
docs.text:
Backpropagation revolutionized machine learning when it was popularized in the 1980s 1. While the core idea (applying chain rule) dates back further, the seminal work by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams demonstrated its practical effectiveness for training multi-layer networks 23.

Key milestones: - 1960s-70s: Early work on automatic differentiation and reverse-mode AD - 1986: Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams 1 popularize backpropagation for neural networks - 1990s: Challenges with deep networks, vanishing gradients - 2006: Hinton's deep belief networks reignite interest - 2012: AlexNet uses backprop + GPUs to win ImageNet, launching deep learning era 4 - Today: Backpropagation trains networks with billions of parameters (GPT, BERT, etc.)

The algorithm's elegance lies in its simplicity: it's just the chain rule, systematically applied. Yet this simple idea enables training incredibly complex models that power modern AI 4.

docs.title: Beyond Feedforward Networks
docs.text:
While we've focused on feedforward networks, backpropagation generalizes to other architectures:

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): Backprop through convolution operations using transposed convolutions

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs): Backpropagation through time (BPTT), unrolling the network across time steps

Transformers: Backprop through self-attention mechanisms, layer normalization, and residual connections

Graph Neural Networks: Message passing and aggregation with backprop on graph structures

The fundamental principle remains the same: compute the forward pass, then propagate gradients backward using the chain rule.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Backpropagation is the workhorse algorithm of deep learning, enabling efficient gradient computation through:

  1. Forward pass: Compute outputs and cache intermediate values
  2. Backward pass: Recursively compute errors using \(\delta^{(l)} = (W^{(l+1)})^T \delta^{(l+1)} \odot g'^{(l)}(z^{(l)})\)
  3. Gradient computation: Use \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} (a^{(l-1)})^T\)
  4. Parameter update: Apply gradient descent or variants

The algorithm's \(O(W)\) complexity (linear in number of weights) makes training deep networks feasible. Combined with powerful hardware (GPUs, TPUs) and modern optimizers, backpropagation has enabled the deep learning revolution 23.

  1. David E. Rumelhart, Geoffrey E. Hinton, and Ronald J. Williams. Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Nature, 323(6088):533–536, 1986. doi:10.1038/323533a0. ↩↩↩

  2. Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. Deep Learning. MIT Press, 2016. URL: https://www.deeplearningbook.org/. ↩↩

  3. Michael A. Nielsen. Neural Networks and Deep Learning. Determination Press, 2015. URL: http://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com/. ↩↩

  4. Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey Hinton. Deep learning. Nature, 521(7553):436–444, 2015. doi:10.1038/nature14539. ↩↩

docs.title: Understanding Neural Networks: An Intuitive yet Precise Introduction
docs.text:
Neural networks have become a defining technology of modern artificial intelligence, powering everything from real-time translation systems to autonomous vehicles and financial forecasting engines. Despite their widespread use, these models often seem surrounded by an aura of mystery. In reality, neural networks are elegant mathematical constructs inspired by the way biological neurons process information. The goal of this article is to show a bit of neural networks by walking you through their structure and core ideas, while maintaining enough technical depth to appreciate how they truly work.

At the heart of any neural network lies the notion of a transformation, defined to as the raw input data which is progressively converted into a meaningful output through layers of interconnected computational units. Each of these units, called neurons, performs a simple operation: it computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a nonlinear activation function. Although this operation is elementary on its own, stacking many such units together produces a powerful system capable of approximating highly complex relationships.

To visualize a compact example, consider the diagram below. It shows a small feedforward network with three input neurons, a hidden layer of three neurons, and a single output neuron. Information flows from left to right through weighted connections. Each weight \(w_{i,j}\) depicts the weight between node \(i\) in previous layer and node \(j\) in current layer.

The structure of a neural network is organized into layers. The input layer receives numerical features—values that encode whatever phenomena the model is meant to analyze. These values pass into the first hidden layer, where each neuron computes a quantity of the form

\[ z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b, \]

which represents a linear combination of inputs (x_i) with weights (w_i) and bias (b). The output (z) is then fed through a nonlinear activation function such as the sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, or the ubiquitous rectified linear unit (ReLU). This nonlinearity is crucial: without it, no matter how many layers we stack, the model would collapse into a single linear transformation and lose all expressive power.

What's ReLU?

The ReLU activation is defined as

\[ \text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z). \]

While seemingly simple, its effect on training dynamics is profound. Because it avoids saturation for positive values, gradients propagate more efficiently, allowing deeper networks to converge more reliably.

As information propagates forward across layers—hence the term feedforward network—each transformation progressively distills structure from the data. Early layers often capture general patterns, while deeper layers specialize in finer details. Ultimately, the final layer condenses all this processed information into an output: a decision, a prediction, or a continuous value depending on the task.

Training a neural network means adjusting its weights so that its output becomes increasingly aligned with known examples. This optimization typically uses gradient-based methods such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The fundamental idea is to compute how a small change in each weight influences the network’s error, a procedure formalized by the backpropagation algorithm. By iteratively applying these updates across many data samples, the network learns an internal representation that captures the essential patterns underlying the input.

Tip

Backpropagation is not a new algorithm; its mathematical foundation is simply an application of the chain rule from calculus. What makes it powerful is the way it systematically decomposes the network’s output error into contributions attributable to each parameter, enabling efficient optimization even in very deep architectures.

When viewed from a higher vantage point, neural networks are universal function approximators: they are capable of representing an astonishing range of input–output relationships with arbitrary precision, given enough capacity and training data. This flexibility explains why they have become foundational tools in natural language processing, computer vision, reinforcement learning, and numerous applied domains.

Yet it is worth noting that neural networks are not magical black boxes. They are structured mathematical models whose mechanics are accessible and interpretable with the right conceptual framing. Although large-scale neural architectures—such as those used in modern generative AI—contain billions of parameters and require sophisticated training pipelines, the principles underpinning them remain the same as in the small network depicted earlier.

Understanding those principles is the first step toward leveraging neural networks effectively, whether for academic research, practical engineering, or exploratory curiosity. Mastery begins with grasping these fundamentals, and from there, the possibilities expand dramatically.

docs.title: Supervised Learning
docs.text: This section explores supervised learning methods, including classification, regression, and evaluation metrics.

docs.title: Unsupervised Learning
docs.text: This section covers the fundamentals and advanced topics in unsupervised learning, including clustering, dimensionality reduction, and anomaly detection.

docs.title: Computer Science
docs.text: Welcome to the Computer Science section. Here, we explore foundational concepts and algorithms that underpin modern computation, with a focus on methods that are essential for problem-solving and artificial intelligence.

docs.title: Algorithmic Design
docs.text:
Algorithmic design is the discipline of constructing principled, efficient procedures for solving computational problems. Where the analysis of algorithms asks how fast or how much memory a given algorithm uses, design asks the earlier question: how do we construct an algorithm in the first place? The two questions are inseparable in practice — a well-chosen design paradigm both structures the solution and determines its complexity.

The field rests on the observation that most computational problems, however superficially different their domains, share deep structural properties that admit recurring solution strategies. Recognising which paradigm applies to a problem — and why — is the central skill of algorithm design. Kleinberg and Tardos 1 organise the field around a small number of such paradigms as a pedagogical framework; Skiena 2 emphasises the design manual perspective, cataloguing problem types and the techniques known to work for each; Cormen et al. 3 provide the rigorous mathematical treatment. Russell and Norvig 4 extend this into AI search.

docs.title: Three Orthogonal Axes of Classification
docs.text:
A persistent source of confusion in the literature is that algorithms are classified along three independent axes that are logically distinct but are often conflated:

Axis Question answered Example Problem domain What kind of data or structure does the problem operate on? Binary search → sorted array Design paradigm What algorithmic strategy is used to construct the solution? Binary search → divide and conquer Search strategy How much knowledge about the goal does the algorithm use? A* → informed (heuristic) search

The same algorithm can be described simultaneously from all three axes: binary search lives in the data-structures search domain, uses the divide and conquer paradigm, and is deterministic (not a search-space algorithm). A lives in the state-space / AI search domain, uses the heuristic cost-based paradigm, and is informed*. Conflating these axes — e.g. calling best-first search a "paradigm" when it is really a search strategy — leads to incoherent comparisons 41.

docs.title: I. By Problem Domain
docs.text: Classifying algorithms by the kind of data or structure they operate on is the most natural starting point. It maps directly to course syllabi (data structures, graph theory, optimisation) and tells you which data representation is assumed 32.

docs.title: 1. Searching in Data Structures
docs.text:
These algorithms search for a target element within an explicitly stored, structured collection. The key characteristic is that the data is enumerable and indexable — elements can be accessed by position or key in \(O(1)\).

Algorithm Data requirement Worst-case cost Linear search None (unsorted sequence) \(O(n)\) Binary search Sorted array \(O(\log n)\) Hash table lookup Hash function, load factor \(< 1\) \(O(1)\) expected

docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text: The paradigm case for searching in data structures is binary search: given a sorted array \(A[0..n-1]\) and a target \(t\), it locates \(t\) — or confirms its absence — in \(O(\log_2 n)\) comparisons. At each step it computes the midpoint \(m_k = \ell_k + \lfloor (h_k - \ell_k) / 2 \rfloor\) and eliminates half the remaining interval by comparing \(A[m_k]\) with \(t\). From the design perspective it is a textbook instance of divide and conquer (Axis II); from the search-strategy perspective it is deterministic and uninformed (it uses no knowledge of where \(t\) might be within the sorted range beyond the sorted-order invariant).

docs.title: Linear Search
docs.text: Linear (sequential) search scans \(A\) left to right, comparing each element with \(t\) in turn. It requires no precondition on \(A\) and costs \(O(n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Although dominated by binary search on sorted data, it is optimal for unsorted data and is the correct choice when the collection is small, unsorted, or stored in a linked structure that does not support random access 3.

docs.title: 2. Sorting Algorithms
docs.text:
Sorting algorithms impose a total order on an unordered sequence. They are foundational because many other algorithms — binary search, Kruskal's MST, many DP formulations — require sorted input.

Algorithm Best case Average case Worst case Space Stable? Merge sort \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n)\) Yes Quick sort \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n^2)\) \(O(\log n)\) No Heap sort \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(1)\) No

docs.title: Merge Sort (article coming soon)
docs.text: Merge sort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each, and merges them in \(O(n)\) time. The recurrence \(T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)\) solves to \(T(n) = O(n \log n)\) by the Master Theorem (see Divide and Conquer below). It is the canonical stable, comparison-based sort and the prototype for external sorting, where data does not fit in RAM 3.

docs.title: 3. Graph Algorithms
docs.text:
Graph algorithms operate on \(G = (V, E)\) where \(V\) is a set of nodes and \(E \subseteq V \times V\) is a set of edges. They model road networks, social graphs, dependency graphs, and state spaces.

Algorithm Problem Complexity BFS Unweighted shortest paths, reachability \(O(V + E)\) DFS Connectivity, topological sort, cycle detection \(O(V + E)\) Dijkstra Weighted shortest paths (non-negative weights) \(O((V + E) \log V)\) Kruskal / Prim Minimum spanning tree \(O(E \log E)\) / \(O((V + E) \log V)\)

docs.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) (article coming soon)
docs.text: BFS explores \(G\) layer by layer from a source \(s\), using a FIFO queue. It visits all nodes at distance \(d\) from \(s\) before visiting any node at distance \(d+1\), and therefore finds the shortest path (minimum number of edges) between \(s\) and every reachable node in \(O(V + E)\) time. From Axis II, BFS is an uninformed search with no priority ordering beyond the FIFO queue. It is the foundation of Dijkstra's algorithm (which adds a cost-weighted priority queue) and of bidirectional search 31.

docs.title: 4. Optimisation Algorithms
docs.text:
Optimisation algorithms seek the best feasible solution under a cost metric and a set of constraints. Unlike graph algorithms, the solution need not be a path — it may be a subset, assignment, schedule, or flow.

Problem Representative algorithm Notes Shortest path Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford Greedy / DP respectively 0/1 Knapsack DP table NP-hard; DP is pseudo-polynomial Interval scheduling Greedy earliest-deadline Polynomial, optimal Maximum flow Ford–Fulkerson, Edmonds–Karp Reduces to LP

docs.title: Knapsack (DP version) (article coming soon)
docs.text: The 0/1 knapsack problem asks: given \(n\) items with values \(v_i\) and weights \(w_i\), and a capacity \(W\), which subset maximises total value subject to total weight \(\leq W\)? The greedy strategy (take items by value-per-weight ratio) is optimal for the fractional knapsack but not for the 0/1 variant. Dynamic programming solves it in \(O(nW)\) time by filling a table \(\text{dp}[i][c]\) = maximum value using items \(1..i\) with capacity \(c\). This is pseudo-polynomial: exponential in the bit length of \(W\), so the problem remains NP-hard in the strong sense 31.

docs.title: 5. State-Space / AI Search
docs.text:
State-space search algorithms navigate an implicitly defined graph whose nodes are configurations (states) of a problem, and whose edges are actions or transitions. Unlike data-structure search, the graph is not stored — it is generated on the fly during exploration. This is the setting studied intensively in artificial intelligence 45.

Algorithm Completeness Optimal? Information used BFS Yes (finite) Yes (unit cost) None DFS No (infinite) No None Uniform-cost search Yes Yes Edge costs only Greedy best-first Yes (finite) No \(h(n)\) only A* Yes Yes (admissible \(h\)) \(g(n) + h(n)\) Iterative deepening Yes Yes (unit cost) None

docs.title: Greedy Best-First Search
docs.text: Greedy best-first search orders its open list by \(h(n)\) — the heuristic estimate of cost from \(n\) to the goal — alone, with no accounting for the cost already paid to reach \(n\). It is fast when \(h\) is accurate but sacrifices optimality: it may return a path that is longer (more expensive) than the shortest one because it cannot distinguish cheap-to-reach nodes from expensive ones that happen to look close to the goal. From Axis II it is a greedy algorithm; from Axis III it is informed search 46.

docs.title: A*
docs.text: A* combines the cost paid so far, \(g(n)\), with the heuristic, \(h(n)\), into the evaluation function \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\). When \(h\) is admissible — never overestimating the true cost to the goal — A* is guaranteed to expand the minimum number of nodes needed to confirm optimality among all algorithms with the same heuristic information 76. It is both an informed search strategy (Axis III) and a heuristic cost-based paradigm (Axis II).

docs.title: II. By Design Paradigm
docs.text: The design paradigm describes the structural strategy used to build the algorithm, independent of the domain. This is the deeper classification: two algorithms can operate on completely different data (one on arrays, one on graphs) yet share the same paradigm — and therefore the same correctness proof technique and the same complexity analysis tools 13.

docs.title: 1. Divide and Conquer
docs.text:
Divide and conquer splits an input of size \(n\) into \(a \geq 2\) sub-problems each of size \(n/b\), solves them recursively, and combines the results in \(O(n^k)\) time. The total work satisfies the recurrence

\[ \begin{equation} T(n) = a\,T\!\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) + O(n^k) \label{eq:master} \end{equation} \]

whose solution is given by the Master Theorem 3:

\[ T(n) = \begin{cases} O(n^k) & \text{if } a < b^k \\ O(n^k \log n) & \text{if } a = b^k \\ O(n^{\log_b a}) & \text{if } a > b^k \end{cases} \] Variables in the Master Theorem Symbol Meaning \(n\) Size of the input \(a \geq 1\) Number of recursive sub-calls \(b > 1\) Factor by which input size is reduced at each level \(k \geq 0\) Exponent in the combine step cost, i.e. \(O(n^k)\) \(T(n)\) Total time cost as a function of \(n\)

Algorithms in this paradigm: binary search (\(a=1, b=2, k=0\)), merge sort (\(a=2, b=2, k=1\)), quick sort (expected), Strassen's matrix multiplication (\(a=7, b=2, k=2\)), FFT, closest-pair 1.

docs.title: 2. Greedy Algorithms
docs.text:
A greedy algorithm builds a solution incrementally by making the locally optimal choice at each step, never reconsidering past decisions. Correctness is proved by one of two standard techniques:

  • Greedy stays ahead: for every prefix of the greedy solution, it is at least as good as the corresponding prefix of any other feasible solution.
  • Exchange argument: any optimal solution can be transformed step by step into the greedy solution without losing quality 1.

Key concept — Greedy-choice property: a globally optimal solution can be assembled from locally optimal choices. This property must be proved; it is not universally true.

Algorithms in this paradigm: Kruskal's MST, Prim's MST, Dijkstra's shortest path (non-negative weights), Huffman coding, interval scheduling maximisation, fractional knapsack, greedy best-first search.

docs.title: 3. Dynamic Programming
docs.text:
Dynamic programming (DP) applies when a problem exhibits two structural properties 31:

  • Optimal substructure: an optimal solution to the full problem contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems.
  • Overlapping sub-problems: the same sub-problems recur in a naive recursive decomposition.

When both hold, sub-problem solutions are stored in a table (bottom-up) or cache (top-down memoisation) and retrieved in \(O(1)\). If there are \(P\) distinct sub-problems each solvable in \(O(W)\) given prior answers, total cost is \(O(P \cdot W)\) — often polynomial where naive enumeration is exponential.

Algorithms in this paradigm: Bellman–Ford shortest paths, Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, sequence alignment (Needleman–Wunsch), matrix-chain multiplication, optimal BSTs, Viterbi algorithm 2.

docs.title: 4. Backtracking
docs.text:
Backtracking is a systematic exhaustive-search strategy that constructs a solution incrementally and prunes partial candidates the moment they are found to violate a feasibility constraint or cannot possibly lead to a better complete solution. The search operates on an implicit tree of partial solutions; pruning eliminates entire subtrees without enumerating them.

Constraint propagation (arc consistency, forward checking) and ordering heuristics (MRV — minimum remaining values) substantially reduce the effective tree size in practice 4.

Algorithms in this paradigm: N-queens, Sudoku solving, graph colouring, SAT solving (DPLL), subset-sum.

docs.title: 5. Branch and Bound
docs.text:
Branch and bound extends backtracking to optimisation: the algorithm maintains an incumbent (best solution found so far) and computes a lower bound on the cost of any completion of a partial solution. A subtree is bounded — pruned — when its lower bound exceeds the incumbent, since no completion can improve on the current best.

The tightness of the lower bound determines efficiency, and best-first node selection (expand the node with the lowest bound) tends to find good incumbents early, maximising pruning 32.

Algorithms in this paradigm: TSP exact solvers, integer linear programming, vehicle routing.

docs.title: 6. Randomised Algorithms
docs.text:
Randomised algorithms introduce deliberate randomness, trading deterministic worst-case guarantees for better expected behaviour or probabilistic correctness.

  • Las Vegas: always correct; running time is a random variable. Example: randomised quicksort (expected \(O(n \log n)\), worst case \(O(n^2)\)).
  • Monte Carlo: fixed or bounded time; correct with high probability. Example: Miller–Rabin primality testing.

Algorithms in this paradigm: randomised quicksort, randomised BSTs, skip lists, Karger's min-cut, Miller–Rabin, randomised approximate counting 13.

docs.title: 7. Approximation Algorithms
docs.text:
For NP-hard optimisation problems, exact polynomial-time solutions are believed impossible. Approximation algorithms run in polynomial time and return a solution within a provable factor \(\alpha \geq 1\) of the optimum:

\[ \begin{equation} \frac{\text{ALG}(I)}{\text{OPT}(I)} \leq \alpha \quad \forall\, \text{instances } I \label{eq:approx_ratio} \end{equation} \] Variables in the approximation ratio Symbol Meaning \(I\) A specific problem instance \(\text{ALG}(I)\) Cost returned by the approximation algorithm \(\text{OPT}(I)\) Cost of the exact optimal solution \(\alpha \geq 1\) Approximation ratio; \(\alpha = 1\) is exact

Algorithms in this paradigm: 2-approximation vertex cover, \((1-1/e)\)-approximation max coverage, PTAS/FPTAS for knapsack, \(O(\log n)\)-approximation set cover, greedy TSP 1.

docs.title: 8. Problem Reductions
docs.text: A reduction \(A \leq_p B\) is a polynomial-time transformation of any input to \(A\) into an input to \(B\) that preserves yes/no answers. Reductions are used both to design algorithms (reduce a new problem to a solved one) and to prove hardness (if \(A\) is NP-hard and \(A \leq_p B\), then \(B\) is NP-hard) 31.

docs.title: III. By Search Strategy
docs.text: This axis classifies algorithms by how much knowledge about the goal they exploit during exploration. It is most relevant for state-space / AI search but also illuminates data-structure algorithms 4.

docs.title: 1. Uninformed (Blind) Search
docs.text:
Uninformed algorithms explore the state space without any domain-specific guidance about where the goal might be. The only information used is the structure of the graph and, where applicable, edge costs.

Algorithm Frontier structure Completeness Optimal? BFS FIFO queue Yes (finite) Yes (unit cost) DFS LIFO stack No (infinite graphs) No Uniform-cost search Min-priority queue on \(g(n)\) Yes Yes Iterative deepening (IDS) DFS with depth limit Yes Yes (unit cost)

docs.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
docs.text: BFS uses a FIFO queue to explore nodes layer by layer from the source. Because every node at depth \(d\) is visited before any at depth \(d+1\), BFS finds the shallowest (minimum-hop) path to the goal. It is complete on finite graphs and optimal for unit-cost edges, but its \(O(b^d)\) memory consumption is prohibitive for deep goals with large branching factors. IDS achieves the same optimal, complete guarantee as BFS with only \(O(bd)\) memory by iterating DFS with increasing depth limits 43.

docs.title: 2. Informed (Heuristic) Search
docs.text:
Informed algorithms use a domain-specific heuristic function \(h(n)\) — an estimate of the cost from \(n\) to the goal — to bias exploration toward promising regions of the state space. The quality of \(h\) determines how much the algorithm improves over blind search.

Algorithm Priority key Optimal? Notes Greedy best-first \(h(n)\) No Fast; may find sub-optimal path A* \(g(n) + h(n)\) Yes (admissible \(h\)) Optimal and complete Weighted A* \(g(n) + w \cdot h(n)\), \(w>1\) \(w\)-approximate Speed–quality trade-off IDA* \(f = g + h\) with iterative threshold Yes \(O(bd)\) memory

A heuristic \(h(n)\) is admissible if \(h(n) \leq h^*(n)\) for all nodes \(n\), where \(h^*(n)\) is the true optimal cost to the goal. Admissibility is the condition under which A* is guaranteed to return an optimal solution. Pearl 6 proves that with a near-perfect heuristic the expected expansion count grows polynomially with path length, rather than exponentially as in blind search.

docs.title: Choosing a Paradigm
docs.text:
No single rule determines the right technique for every problem. The following questions guide the choice:

  1. Does the problem have optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems? → Dynamic programming.
  2. Does a local greedy choice provably lead to global optimality? → Greedy algorithm.
  3. Is the input recursively divisible into independent sub-problems? → Divide and conquer.
  4. Is the problem a constraint satisfaction or combinatorial search? → Backtracking or branch and bound.
  5. Is the problem NP-hard and exact optimality not required? → Approximation algorithm or heuristic.
  6. Can randomness break worst-case patterns? → Randomised algorithm.
  7. Can the problem be transformed into one already solved efficiently? → Reduction.
  8. Is domain-specific distance information available? → Informed search (greedy best-first, A*).

Skiena 2 provides a problem-type catalogue matched to techniques; Kleinberg and Tardos 1 develop each paradigm from first principles with formal proofs; Cormen et al. 3 give the standard mathematical treatment across all paradigms.

docs.title: Graph Algorithms
docs.text: Graph algorithms operate on \(G = (V, E)\) where \(V\) is a finite set of vertices and \(E \subseteq V \times V\) is a set of edges. They model an enormous range of real-world structures: road networks, circuit boards, dependency trees, social networks, and compiler flow graphs.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Algorithm Problem Paradigm Complexity Breadth-First Search Reachability, unweighted shortest paths Uninformed traversal \(O(V + E)\) Depth-First Search Connectivity, topological sort, SCC Uninformed traversal \(O(V + E)\) Dijkstra's Algorithm Weighted shortest paths (non-negative) Greedy \(O((V + E) \log V)\) Kruskal's Algorithm Minimum spanning tree Greedy (Union-Find) \(O(E \log E)\) Prim's Algorithm Minimum spanning tree Greedy (priority queue) \(O((V + E) \log V)\)

docs.title: Key Data Representations
docs.text:
• Adjacency list: \(O(V + E)\) space; preferred for sparse graphs. Edge traversal costs \(O(\deg(v))\) per vertex.
  • Adjacency matrix: \(O(V^2)\) space; preferred for dense graphs and algorithms that test edge existence in \(O(1)\) (e.g. Floyd–Warshall).
  • Edge list: \(O(E)\) space; natural for Kruskal's algorithm, which sorts edges.

docs.title: Breadth-First Search
docs.text:
Breadth-first search (BFS) is one of the two fundamental graph traversal strategies, the other being depth-first search. Starting from a source vertex \(s\), BFS explores all vertices at distance 1 (direct neighbours), then all at distance 2, and so on in expanding concentric shells, using a FIFO queue to maintain the exploration frontier. This layer-by-layer order guarantees that BFS finds the shortest path (minimum number of edges) from \(s\) to every reachable vertex in an unweighted graph 12.

BFS also serves as the foundation for more sophisticated algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm replaces the FIFO queue with a priority queue, and the A* algorithm adds a heuristic. Edmonds–Karp maximum flow uses BFS to find augmenting paths.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given a graph \(G = (V, E)\) and a source vertex \(s \in V\), compute:

  1. The shortest-path distance \(d[v]\) from \(s\) to every vertex \(v\) reachable from \(s\).
  2. A shortest-path tree rooted at \(s\) via predecessor pointers \(\pi[v]\).
\[ \begin{equation} d[v] = \min\{ |P| : P \text{ is a path from } s \text{ to } v \text{ in } G \} \label{eq:bfs_distance} \end{equation} \]

where \(|P|\) denotes the number of edges in path \(P\).

Variables Symbol Meaning \(G = (V, E)\) Graph with vertex set \(V\) and edge set \(E\) \(s\) Source vertex \(d[v]\) Shortest-path distance (edge count) from \(s\) to \(v\) \(\pi[v]\) Predecessor of \(v\) on the shortest path from \(s\) \(\text{color}[v]\) WHITE = undiscovered, GRAY = in queue, BLACK = finished \(Q\) FIFO queue holding the current frontier

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
BFS(G, s):
  for each vertex u ∈ V \ {s}:
    color[u] = WHITE;  d[u] = ∞;  π[u] = NIL
  color[s] = GRAY;  d[s] = 0;  π[s] = NIL
  Q = empty queue
  ENQUEUE(Q, s)
  while Q ≠ ∅:
    u = DEQUEUE(Q)
    for each v ∈ Adj[u]:
      if color[v] = WHITE:
        color[v] = GRAY
        d[v] = d[u] + 1
        π[v] = u
        ENQUEUE(Q, v)
    color[u] = BLACK

docs.title: Correctness: Shortest-Path Guarantee
docs.text:
BFS produces correct shortest-path distances. The key invariant on the queue \(Q\) at any point: if the queue contains vertices \(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_r\) (in FIFO order), then

\[ d[v_1] \leq d[v_2] \leq \cdots \leq d[v_r] \leq d[v_1] + 1 \]

That is, the queue contains at most two consecutive distance layers. This ensures vertices are settled in non-decreasing distance order, so the first time BFS reaches \(v\), it does so via a shortest path 1.

Proof sketch: by induction on \(d[v]\). When \(v\) is first enqueued, it is enqueued from some \(u\) with \(d[u] = d[v] - 1\). By induction \(d[u]\) is correct, so \(d[v] = d[u] + 1\) equals the true shortest-path distance.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Phase Cost Initialisation \(O(V)\) Queue operations \(O(V)\) total (each vertex enqueued exactly once) Edge relaxations \(O(E)\) total (each edge considered exactly twice in undirected graphs) Total \(O(V + E)\)

Space: \(O(V)\) for the queue, colour, distance, and predecessor arrays.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Completeness: BFS visits every vertex reachable from \(s\). It is complete on all finite, connected graphs and finds all reachable vertices in any finite graph.
  • Optimality: BFS finds shortest paths measured by edge count. For weighted graphs, use Dijkstra or Uniform-Cost Search.
  • Tree structure: the predecessor pointers \(\pi\) define a BFS tree (also called the shortest-path tree). The unique path from \(s\) to \(v\) in this tree is a shortest path in \(G\).

docs.title: Bipartiteness Testing
docs.text: BFS can test whether \(G\) is bipartite (2-colourable) in \(O(V + E)\): colour \(s\) white, colour all neighbours black, all their neighbours white, and so on. If a conflict arises — an edge between two vertices of the same colour — then an odd-length cycle exists and \(G\) is not bipartite. Otherwise, the colouring witnesses bipartiteness 1.

docs.title: Multi-Source BFS
docs.text: If several sources \(S \subseteq V\) are given, initialise all with \(d[s] = 0\) and enqueue all simultaneously before the main loop. This computes shortest distances from the nearest source to every vertex in \(O(V + E)\) — useful for problems like "nearest fire station" or "nearest safe cell" on a grid.

docs.title: Bidirectional BFS
docs.text: Run BFS simultaneously from \(s\) and the goal \(g\), alternating frontier expansions. Stop when the two frontiers meet. In a graph with branching factor \(b\) and shortest path of length \(d\), standard BFS visits \(O(b^d)\) nodes while bidirectional BFS visits \(O(b^{d/2})\) — exponentially fewer. Used in social-network distance queries and some route planners.

docs.title: 0-1 BFS
docs.text: On graphs where edges have weight 0 or 1, replace the FIFO queue with a deque (double-ended queue): edges of weight 0 push to the front; edges of weight 1 push to the back. This computes shortest paths in \(O(V + E)\) without a priority queue, unlike Dijkstra.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Shortest paths in unweighted graphs (road networks with uniform edge costs, word ladder)
  • Connected components of undirected graphs
  • Bipartiteness testing
  • Web crawling (visit all pages within \(k\) hops)
  • Social network diameter estimation
  • Edmonds–Karp maximum flow (BFS augmenting paths)
  • Level-order traversal of trees

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Memory: BFS stores the entire frontier in the queue. In graphs with large branching factor \(b\) and goal at depth \(d\), the queue may contain \(O(b^d)\) nodes, making it impractical for deep goals. Iterative deepening achieves the same correctness with \(O(bd)\) memory.
  • Unweighted only: for weighted graphs, BFS ignores edge costs and may return a path that minimises hops but not total weight. Use Dijkstra for weighted shortest paths.

docs.title: Depth-First Search
docs.text:
Depth-first search (DFS) explores a graph by going as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking. From a source vertex it follows an edge to an unvisited neighbour, then an edge from that neighbour, and so on until it reaches a vertex with no unvisited neighbours, at which point it backtracks to the most recent vertex that still has unexplored edges. DFS runs in \(O(V + E)\) and, unlike BFS, uses \(O(V)\) stack depth (recursion stack or explicit stack) rather than \(O(V)\) queue width.

DFS is remarkably versatile: it underpins topological sorting, strongly connected components (Tarjan's / Kosaraju's algorithms), cycle detection, and articulation points / bridges. It is the implicit engine of recursive backtracking algorithms 12.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given a directed or undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\), a DFS of \(G\) assigns to each vertex \(v\) a discovery time \(d[v]\) and a finish time \(f[v]\) satisfying

\[ \begin{equation} d[v] < f[v] \quad \text{and} \quad \text{for any two vertices } u, v, \text{ either } [d[u], f[u]] \text{ and } [d[v], f[v]] \text{ are disjoint or one contains the other} \label{eq:dfs_parenthesis} \end{equation} \]

This is the parenthesis theorem: the DFS exploration intervals are properly nested.

Variables Symbol Meaning \(G = (V, E)\) Graph with vertex set \(V\) and edge set \(E\) \(d[v]\) Discovery time of vertex \(v\) \(f[v]\) Finish time of vertex \(v\) (after all descendants processed) \(\pi[v]\) DFS predecessor (parent in DFS tree) \(\text{color}[v]\) WHITE = undiscovered, GRAY = on stack, BLACK = finished \(\text{time}\) Global clock incremented on each discovery and finish

docs.title: Recursive DFS
docs.text:
DFS(G):
  for each vertex u ∈ V:
    color[u] = WHITE;  π[u] = NIL
  time = 0
  for each vertex u ∈ V:
    if color[u] = WHITE:
      DFS-VISIT(G, u)

DFS-VISIT(G, u):
  time = time + 1
  d[u] = time
  color[u] = GRAY
  for each v ∈ Adj[u]:
    if color[v] = WHITE:
      π[v] = u
      DFS-VISIT(G, v)
  color[u] = BLACK
  time = time + 1
  f[u] = time

docs.title: Iterative DFS (Explicit Stack)
docs.text:
DFS-ITERATIVE(G, s):
  stack = {s}
  while stack ≠ ∅:
    u = stack.pop()
    if color[u] ≠ BLACK:
      color[u] = BLACK
      for each v ∈ Adj[u] (reversed):
        if color[v] = WHITE:
          stack.push(v)
Iterative vs. recursive DFS — edge classification

The iterative version above does not faithfully reproduce the discovery/finish timestamps of recursive DFS and therefore cannot be used directly for topological sort or SCC without modification. The recursive version is canonical for algorithmic analysis.

docs.title: Edge Classification
docs.text:
DFS classifies each edge \((u, v)\) by the colours of \(u\) and \(v\) at the moment the edge is first examined:

Edge type Condition Directed/Undirected Tree edge \(v\) is WHITE Both Back edge \(v\) is GRAY (ancestor of \(u\)) Both; indicates a cycle in directed graphs Forward edge \(v\) is BLACK, \(d[u] < d[v]\) Directed only Cross edge \(v\) is BLACK, \(d[u] > d[v]\) Directed only

In an undirected graph, DFS produces only tree edges and back edges.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Phase Cost Initialisation \(O(V)\) DFS-VISIT calls (total) \(O(V)\) (once per vertex) Edge examination (total) \(O(E)\) Total \(O(V + E)\)

Space: \(O(V)\) for the colour, timestamp, and predecessor arrays plus \(O(V)\) call stack in the worst case (a path graph).

docs.title: Topological Sort
docs.text:
A topological sort of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge \((u, v)\), \(u\) appears before \(v\). DFS computes it in \(O(V + E)\): run DFS and insert each vertex at the front of a linked list as it is finished (i.e. as it becomes BLACK). The resulting list is a topological order 1.

TOPO-SORT(G):
  run DFS(G)
  as each vertex u finishes, insert u at head of list L
  return L

Correctness: if \((u, v) \in E\), then \(f[v] < f[u]\) (because DFS finishes all descendants of \(u\) before \(u\) itself finishes), so \(u\) precedes \(v\) in \(L\).

docs.title: Cycle Detection
docs.text: A directed graph contains a cycle if and only if DFS produces a back edge (an edge to a GRAY, i.e. currently-on-stack, vertex). In undirected graphs, any repeated visit via a non-tree edge indicates a cycle.

docs.title: Strongly Connected Components (Kosaraju's Algorithm)
docs.text:
1. Run DFS on \(G\); record finish times.
  2. Transpose \(G\) (reverse all edges) to get \(G^T\).
  3. Run DFS on \(G^T\), processing vertices in decreasing finish-time order.
  4. Each DFS tree in step 3 is a strongly connected component.

Total cost: \(O(V + E)\) 1.

docs.title: Articulation Points and Bridges
docs.text: An articulation point is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph. A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph. Both can be found in \(O(V + E)\) using DFS and the notion of low values (the lowest discovery time reachable from a subtree via at most one back edge).

docs.title: Comparison with BFS
docs.text: Property DFS BFS Data structure Stack (LIFO) Queue (FIFO) Space \(O(V)\) stack \(O(V)\) queue Shortest paths No Yes (unweighted) Topological sort Yes No (directly) SCC, bridges Yes No (directly) Cycle detection Yes (back edge) Yes (re-encounter)

docs.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
docs.text: Dijkstra's algorithm, published by Edsger W. Dijkstra in 1959, solves the single-source shortest-path (SSSP) problem on a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. Starting from a source vertex \(s\), it determines the minimum-cost path to every vertex reachable from \(s\) in \(O((V + E) \log V)\) time (with a binary heap). Dijkstra's is arguably the most important greedy algorithm in graph theory: it underpins GPS navigation, internet routing protocols (OSPF), public transit planning, and network flow preprocessing 12.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given a weighted directed graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) where \(w : E \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) assigns non-negative real weights to edges, and a source \(s \in V\), find, for every vertex \(v \in V\):

\[ \begin{equation} \delta(s, v) = \min\left\{ \sum_{e \in P} w(e) : P \text{ is a path from } s \text{ to } v \right\} \label{eq:dijkstra_delta} \end{equation} \]

Set \(\delta(s, v) = \infty\) if \(v\) is not reachable from \(s\).

Variables Symbol Meaning \(G = (V, E, w)\) Weighted graph; \(w(u,v)\) is edge cost \(s\) Source vertex \(\delta(s, v)\) True shortest-path distance from \(s\) to \(v\) \(d[v]\) Current estimate of shortest distance to \(v\) \(\pi[v]\) Predecessor of \(v\) on the estimated shortest path \(S\) Set of vertices whose shortest paths have been finalised \(Q\) Min-priority queue on \(d\) values; contains unsettled vertices

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
Dijkstra's algorithm greedily settles vertices in order of their current distance estimate. It maintains a min-priority queue \(Q\) keyed by \(d[v]\):

DIJKSTRA(G, w, s):
  for each v ∈ V:
    d[v] = ∞;  π[v] = NIL
  d[s] = 0
  Q = V (min-priority queue keyed by d)
  while Q ≠ ∅:
    u = EXTRACT-MIN(Q)        // settles u
    for each v ∈ Adj[u]:
      RELAX(u, v, w)

RELAX(u, v, w):
  if d[v] > d[u] + w(u, v):
    d[v] = d[u] + w(u, v)
    π[v] = u
    DECREASE-KEY(Q, v, d[v])

docs.title: The Greedy Choice
docs.text: At each step, Dijkstra extracts the unsettled vertex \(u\) with the smallest \(d[u]\) estimate and settles it — declares \(d[u]\) final. The key insight is that if all edge weights are non-negative, no future path through an unsettled vertex can improve the cost to \(u\): any such path would first have to pass through a vertex with \(d \geq d[u]\).

docs.title: Correctness: Loop Invariant
docs.text:
At the start of each EXTRACT-MIN, for every vertex \(v \in S\) (already settled):

\(d[v] = \delta(s, v)\)

Proof (sketch): suppose the first vertex incorrectly settled is \(u\), with \(d[u] > \delta(s, u)\). Then there is a true shortest path \(s \leadsto y \to \cdots \to u\) where \(y\) is the last settled vertex on the path and \(( y, \cdots )\) are unsettled. By the inductive hypothesis \(d[y] = \delta(s, y)\) (correct). After relaxing \((y, z)\):

\[d[z] \leq \delta(s, y) + w(y, z) = \delta(s, z)\]

By non-negativity \(\delta(s, z) \leq \delta(s, u) < d[u]\), contradicting the fact that \(u\) was chosen as the minimum-key element over \(z\) 1.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Priority queue EXTRACT-MIN DECREASE-KEY Total Array (linear scan) \(O(V)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(V^2)\) Binary heap \(O(\log V)\) \(O(\log V)\) \(O((V + E) \log V)\) Fibonacci heap \(O(\log V)\) amort. \(O(1)\) amort. \(O(E + V \log V)\)

For sparse graphs (\(E = O(V)\)), the binary-heap implementation gives \(O(V \log V)\). For dense graphs (\(E = O(V^2)\)), the \(O(V^2)\) array version is competitive. Fibonacci heaps achieve the theoretically optimal bound but carry large constants and are rarely used in practice 1.

docs.title: Why Non-Negative Weights?
docs.text:
The greedy settlement step depends critically on the fact that adding an unsettled vertex to a path cannot decrease its cost. If a negative edge \((u, v)\) exists, a path through an unsettled vertex might be cheaper than the current estimate, invalidating the invariant.

Counterexample with negative weight: \(s \to u\) with cost 5, \(s \to v\) with cost 3, \(v \to u\) with cost \(-10\). Dijkstra settles \(v\) first (\(d[v] = 3\)), then settles \(u\) with \(d[u] = 5\) — but the shortest path is \(s \to v \to u\) with cost \(-7\). Dijkstra fails.

For graphs with negative weights (but no negative cycles), use Bellman–Ford (\(O(VE)\)).

docs.title: Relationship to Other Algorithms
docs.text:
Algorithm Priority key Meaning Dijkstra \(d[u]\) (distance from \(s\)) Weighted shortest paths BFS Layer (FIFO queue) Unweighted shortest paths Uniform-Cost Search \(g(n)\) (same as Dijkstra) State-space equivalent A* \(g(n) + h(n)\) Heuristic-guided SSSP Prim's MST Minimum edge weight to tree Minimum spanning tree

Dijkstra and Prim differ only in their priority key: Dijkstra keys on the total path cost, while Prim keys on the single edge weight connecting a vertex to the current tree.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• GPS and mapping services (route planning)
  • Internet routing (OSPF and IS-IS protocols)
  • Flight path optimisation
  • Network delay analysis
  • Preprocessing for bidirectional shortest-path queries
