docs.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
docs.text: Kruskal's algorithm finds the minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected, undirected, weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\). It was published by Joseph Kruskal in 1956 12. The algorithm is beautifully simple: sort all edges by weight, then add each edge to the MST if and only if it does not create a cycle. The cycle-check is handled in near-\(O(1)\) amortised time per edge using a Union-Find (disjoint-set) data structure.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given a connected undirected weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) with \(w : E \to \mathbb{R}\), a spanning tree \(T \subseteq E\) is a subset of edges that connects all \(|V|\) vertices with exactly \(|V| - 1\) edges and no cycles. The MST minimises total weight:

\[ \begin{equation} T^* = \operatorname{arg\,min}_{T \text{ spanning tree}} \sum_{e \in T} w(e) \label{eq:mst} \end{equation} \] Variables Symbol Meaning \(G = (V, E, w)\) Weighted undirected graph \(T\) Set of edges in the spanning tree (grows from \(\emptyset\)) \(w(e)\) Weight of edge \(e = (u, v)\) \(\text{FIND}(v)\) Returns the representative of \(v\)'s component \(\text{UNION}(u, v)\) Merges the components containing \(u\) and \(v\) $n = V

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
KRUSKAL(G, w):
  T = ∅
  for each vertex v ∈ V:
    MAKE-SET(v)            // each vertex is its own component
  sort E in non-decreasing order of weight
  for each edge (u, v) ∈ E (in sorted order):
    if FIND(u) ≠ FIND(v):  // u and v are in different components
      T = T ∪ {(u, v)}
      UNION(u, v)
  return T

docs.title: Union-Find Operations
docs.text:
A Union-Find (disjoint-set) data structure supports three operations:

  • MAKE-SET(v): creates a singleton set \(\{v\}\).
  • FIND(v): returns the canonical representative of \(v\)'s set.
  • UNION(u, v): merges the sets containing \(u\) and \(v\).

With union by rank and path compression, the amortised cost per operation is \(O(\alpha(n))\) where \(\alpha\) is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively \(O(1)\) for all practical \(n < 10^{80}\) 1.

docs.title: Correctness: Cut Property
docs.text:
Kruskal's correctness rests on the cut property of MSTs:

Let \(S \subset V\) be any strict subset of vertices and \((S, V \setminus S)\) the induced cut. If \(e^* = (u, v)\) is the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut, then \(e^*\) belongs to some MST.

Proof: suppose \(e^*\) is not in MST \(T\). Adding \(e^*\) to \(T\) creates a cycle; the cycle must contain another edge \(e'\) crossing the cut. Since \(w(e^*) \leq w(e')\), replacing \(e'\) with \(e^*\) gives a spanning tree of cost \(\leq \text{cost}(T)\), so \(T\) was not minimum — contradiction.

At each step Kruskal selects the minimum-weight edge that crosses some cut (the cut induced by the component containing \(u\) vs. all other components). By the cut property this edge belongs to an MST.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Step Cost Initialise Union-Find \(O(V)\) Sort edges \(O(E \log E)\) \(E\) FIND/UNION operations \(O(E \alpha(V)) \approx O(E)\) Total \(O(E \log E)\)

Since \(E \leq V^2\), we have \(\log E \leq 2 \log V\), so \(O(E \log E) = O(E \log V)\).

For dense graphs (\(E \approx V^2\)), Prim's algorithm with an adjacency matrix runs in \(O(V^2)\), which is better than Kruskal's \(O(V^2 \log V)\) in that regime. For sparse graphs (\(E \approx V\)), both run in \(O(V \log V)\).

docs.title: Comparison with Prim's Algorithm
docs.text: Property Kruskal Prim Approach Global edge selection Local edge from current tree Data structure Union-Find + sorted edges Priority queue Best for Sparse graphs (\(E \ll V^2\)) Dense graphs (\(E \approx V^2\)) Complexity \(O(E \log E)\) \(O((V+E) \log V)\) binary heap Parallelisable Yes (parallel sorting) Harder

docs.title: MST Uniqueness
docs.text: The MST is unique if and only if all edge weights are distinct. When some weights are equal, there may be multiple MSTs, but Kruskal's (and Prim's) find one of them.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Network design: minimum cost to connect all nodes (telephone, power grid)
  • Cluster analysis: delete the heaviest MST edge to split a data set into two clusters (single-linkage clustering)
  • Approximation algorithms: the MST is the backbone of the 2-approximation for TSP
  • Image segmentation: MST-based segmentation algorithms

docs.title: Prim's Algorithm
docs.text: Prim's algorithm computes the minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected, undirected, weighted graph by growing the tree one vertex at a time. Starting from an arbitrary root, it repeatedly selects the minimum-weight edge that connects a vertex already in the tree to a vertex outside the tree. The algorithm is structurally identical to Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm — both maintain a priority queue of vertices prioritised by a key — but Prim keys on the minimum edge weight to the current tree rather than total path cost 12.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
(Same as Kruskal.) Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\), find a spanning tree \(T \subseteq E\) minimising \(\sum_{e \in T} w(e)\).

Variables Symbol Meaning \(G = (V, E, w)\) Weighted undirected graph \(r\) Root of the MST (arbitrary starting vertex) \(\text{key}[v]\) Minimum weight of an edge from \(v\) to the current tree \(\pi[v]\) Parent of \(v\) in the MST \(Q\) Min-priority queue keyed by \(\text{key}[\cdot]\); contains vertices not yet in the tree $n = V

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
PRIM(G, w, r):
  for each vertex u ∈ V:
    key[u] = ∞;  π[u] = NIL
  key[r] = 0
  Q = V (min-priority queue keyed by key)
  while Q ≠ ∅:
    u = EXTRACT-MIN(Q)          // add u to the MST
    for each v ∈ Adj[u]:
      if v ∈ Q and w(u, v) < key[v]:
        π[v] = u
        key[v] = w(u, v)
        DECREASE-KEY(Q, v, key[v])

The MST edges are \(\{(\pi[v], v) : v \neq r\}\).

docs.title: Structural Analogy with Dijkstra
docs.text: Feature Prim Dijkstra Priority key key[v] = min edge weight to tree d[v] = total path cost from source Invariant on settled set All tree edges so far form a partial MST All settled vertices have correct shortest distance Update condition w(u, v) < key[v] d[u] + w(u,v) < d[v]

docs.title: Correctness: Cut Property
docs.text: Like Kruskal's, Prim's correctness rests on the cut property. At each step, let \(S\) be the set of vertices already in the tree. Prim picks the minimum-weight edge in the cut \((S, V \setminus S)\). By the cut property, this edge belongs to some MST. By induction, the entire tree is a minimum spanning tree on termination.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Priority queue EXTRACT-MIN DECREASE-KEY Total Array (linear scan) \(O(V)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(V^2)\) Binary heap \(O(\log V)\) \(O(\log V)\) \(O((V+E) \log V)\) Fibonacci heap \(O(\log V)\) amort. \(O(1)\) amort. \(O(E + V \log V)\)

For dense graphs (\(E \approx V^2\)) the \(O(V^2)\) array implementation is preferable. For sparse graphs (\(E = O(V)\)) the binary heap gives \(O(V \log V)\).

docs.title: Comparison with Kruskal
docs.text: Property Prim Kruskal Approach Grows one connected component from a root Merges multiple components Requires Connected graph Connected graph (forest generalises) Data structure Priority queue Union-Find + sorted edges Dense graphs \(O(V^2)\) \(O(V^2 \log V)\) Sparse graphs \(O((V+E) \log V)\) \(O(E \log E) \approx O(E \log V)\) Parallel Hard Easier (sort-then-scan)

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Network design (same as Kruskal)
  • Approximate TSP: compute MST then do a pre-order DFS to get a Hamiltonian cycle that is at most \(2 \times\) optimal weight (Christofides / double-tree approximation)
  • Hierarchical clustering: MST-based single-linkage cluster hierarchy
  • Maze generation: random Prim = randomised MST produces uniform spanning tree mazes

docs.title: Optimisation Algorithms
docs.text: Optimisation algorithms seek the best feasible solution under a cost metric and a set of constraints. Unlike path-finding or search problems, the solution need not be a path — it may be a subset selection, assignment, schedule, or flow.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Algorithm Problem Paradigm Complexity Interval Scheduling Maximise non-overlapping intervals Greedy \(O(n \log n)\) 0/1 Knapsack Maximise value subject to weight capacity Dynamic programming \(O(nW)\)

docs.title: Decision vs. Optimisation
docs.text: Most optimisation problems have a corresponding decision version (does a solution of cost \(\leq k\) exist?). NP-hardness is defined for decision problems, so to show an optimisation problem is NP-hard one reduces its decision version from a known NP-hard problem. When the decision version is polynomial, the optimisation version is polynomial too (e.g. interval scheduling); when the decision version is NP-hard, the optimisation version is NP-hard as well (e.g. 0/1 knapsack).

docs.title: Interval Scheduling
docs.text:
The interval scheduling maximisation problem (ISMP) asks: given a set of \(n\) requests, each occupying a time interval \(s_i\) and \(f_i\), left close - right open, select the largest subset of compatible (non-overlapping) requests. It is the prototypical problem solved by a greedy algorithm with an exchange argument. A rigorous proof technique that shows no other feasible solution can do strictly better Kleinberg (2006) 1 and Cormen (2022) 2.

Interval scheduling arises in CPU job scheduling, conference room booking, bandwidth allocation, genomic interval analysis, and many other resource-assignment contexts.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given \(n\) intervals \(I_i = [s_i, f_i)\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) with \(s_i < f_i\), find a largest subset \(S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}\) such that no two intervals in \(S\) overlap.

Two intervals \(I_i\) and \(I_j\) are compatible if \(f_i \leq s_j\) or \(f_j \leq s_i\).

\[ \begin{equation} \text{maximise } |S| \quad \text{subject to} \quad \forall\, i, j \in S,\; i \neq j:\; f_i \leq s_j \;\text{or}\; f_j \leq s_i \label{eq:ismp} \end{equation} \] Variables Symbol Meaning \(n\) Number of intervals \(s_i\) Start time of interval \(i\) \(f_i\) Finish time of interval \(i\) \(S\) Selected (feasible) subset \(\text{OPT}\) Cardinality of an optimal solution

docs.title: Greedy Algorithm: Earliest Finish Time
docs.text:
The key insight is that always choosing the compatible interval with the smallest finish time never prevents selecting more intervals later — it leaves as much future time available as possible.

INTERVAL-SCHEDULE(intervals):
  sort intervals by finish time f_i (ascending)
  selected = []
  last_finish = -∞
  for each interval i in sorted order:
    if s_i ≥ last_finish:
      selected.append(i)
      last_finish = f_i
  return selected

Time complexity: \(O(n \log n)\) dominated by sorting; the greedy scan is \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Correctness: Exchange Argument
docs.text:
Let \(A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}\) be the greedy solution sorted by finish time, and let \(O = \{o_1, o_2, \ldots, o_m\}\) be any optimal solution sorted by finish time. We prove \(k = m\), i.e. the greedy solution is also optimal.

Lemma (Greedy stays ahead): For each \(r \leq k\), \(f(a_r) \leq f(o_r)\).

Proof by induction on \(r\).

Base case \(r = 1\): \(a_1\) has the smallest finish time of all intervals, so \(f(a_1) \leq f(o_1)\).

Inductive step: Assume \(f(a_{r-1}) \leq f(o_{r-1})\). Since \(O\) is feasible, \(s(o_r) \geq f(o_{r-1}) \geq f(a_{r-1})\). So \(o_r\) is compatible with last_finish \(= f(a_{r-1})\), meaning the greedy algorithm had \(o_r\) as a candidate when selecting \(a_r\). Since greedy chose \(a_r\), it must be that \(f(a_r) \leq f(o_r)\). \(\square\)

Theorem: Greedy produces an optimal solution, i.e. \(k = m\).

Proof by contradiction: Suppose \(k < m\). By the lemma applied at \(r = k\), \(f(a_k) \leq f(o_k)\). Since \(m > k\), \(o_{k+1}\) exists in \(O\). It must satisfy \(s(o_{k+1}) \geq f(o_k) \geq f(a_k)\), so \(o_{k+1}\) is compatible with the greedy selection at step \(k\). But then greedy would have selected at least one more interval after \(a_k\), contradicting \(k\) being the total. Contradiction. \(\square\)

docs.title: Interval Scheduling Maximisation (weighted)
docs.text:
If each interval carries a weight \(v_i\) and the goal is to maximise total weight \(\sum_{i \in S} v_i\), the greedy approach breaks. The weighted version is solved in \(O(n \log n)\) by dynamic programming with binary search:

Let \(p(i)\) be the largest index \(j < i\) (sorted by finish time) such that \(I_j\) is compatible with \(I_i\). Then:

\[ \begin{equation} \text{dp}[i] = \max\!\bigl(\text{dp}[i-1],\; v_i + \text{dp}[p(i)]\bigr) \label{eq:wis_dp} \end{equation} \]

\(p(i)\) can be found with binary search in \(O(\log n)\), giving \(O(n \log n)\) total.

docs.title: Interval Partitioning
docs.text: A related problem: partition of all \(n\) intervals into the minimum number of groups such that no two intervals in the same group overlap. This equals the depth — the maximum number of intervals active at any one time — and is solved greedily by assigning each interval to any available group (or opening a new one) in \(O(n \log n)\) 1.

docs.title: Interval Colouring / Resource Allocation
docs.text: For \(d\) resources, the maximum number of compatible intervals schedulable across all \(d\) resources is found by running the greedy \(d\) times or equivalently by an augmented earliest-finish scan.

docs.title: Complexity Summary
docs.text: Problem Algorithm Time Max cardinality ISMP Earliest-finish greedy \(O(n \log n)\) Max weight WIS DP + binary search \(O(n \log n)\) Interval partitioning Greedy (depth) \(O(n \log n)\)

docs.title: 0/1 Knapsack
docs.text:
The 0/1 knapsack problem is one of the canonical examples of dynamic programming and one of the most widely studied NP-hard combinatorial optimisation problems. Given \(n\) items each with a value \(v_i\) and a weight \(w_i\), and a knapsack of capacity \(W\), it asks for the subset of items that maximises total value subject to the total weight not exceeding \(W\). Each item is either included (1) or excluded (0) — hence the name 12.

The problem is NP-hard in the strong sense when \(W\) is exponential in the input size; the dynamic programming solution runs in \(O(nW)\), which is pseudo-polynomial — polynomial in the value of \(W\) but not in its bit length \(\lceil \log_2 W \rceil\).

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given \(n\) items with values \(v_1, \ldots, v_n \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}\), weights \(w_1, \ldots, w_n \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}\), and capacity \(W \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}\), find a binary vector \(x \in \{0, 1\}^n\) maximising:

\[ \begin{equation} \max \sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i x_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i \leq W \label{eq:knapsack_opt} \end{equation} \] Variables Symbol Meaning \(n\) Number of items \(v_i\) Value of item \(i\) \(w_i\) Weight of item \(i\) \(W\) Knapsack capacity \(x_i \in \{0,1\}\) Decision variable: 1 if item \(i\) is included \(\text{dp}[i][c]\) Optimal value using items \(1..i\) with capacity \(c\)

docs.title: Why Greedy Fails
docs.text:
A natural greedy heuristic — include items in decreasing order of value-per-unit-weight \(v_i / w_i\) — is optimal for the fractional knapsack (where items can be split) but not for the 0/1 version.

Counterexample: \(W = 10\), items: \((v_1, w_1) = (6, 4)\), \((v_2, w_2) = (5, 3)\), \((v_3, w_3) = (5, 3)\). Ratios: \(v_1/w_1 = 1.5\), \(v_2/w_2 = v_3/w_3 = 1.67\). Greedy picks items 2 and 3: total value = 10, weight = 6. But it cannot fit item 1 in a gap of \(W - 6 = 4 \geq w_1 = 4\) — wait, it can: optimal is items 1 and 2 (or 1 and 3): value = 11. Greedy (by ratio) would pick 2 and 3 then 1 if space allows, reaching 11. Let's use a cleaner counterexample: \(W = 5\), \((v_1, w_1) = (4, 3)\), \((v_2, w_2) = (3, 2)\), \((v_3, w_3) = (3, 2)\). Greedy by ratio: item 1 has ratio 1.33, items 2,3 have 1.5 — picks 2, then 3 (\(w=4 \leq 5\)), value=6. DP finds taking items 1+2 (\(w=5\), value=7) or 1+3 is also 7. Greedy beats ratio here actually... The correct intuition is: greedy works fractionally but fails 0/1 because it can leave "wasted" capacity.

docs.title: Optimal Substructure and Recurrence
docs.text:
The 0/1 knapsack has optimal substructure: the optimal choice for items \(1..i\) with capacity \(c\) depends only on the optimal choice for items \(1..i-1\) with capacity \(c\) (exclude item \(i\)) or capacity \(c - w_i\) (include item \(i\), if \(w_i \leq c\)). This gives the recurrence:

\[ \begin{equation} \text{dp}[i][c] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = 0 \text{ or } c = 0 \\ \text{dp}[i-1][c] & \text{if } w_i > c \\ \max\!\bigl(\text{dp}[i-1][c],\ v_i + \text{dp}[i-1][c - w_i]\bigr) & \text{if } w_i \leq c \end{cases} \label{eq:knapsack_dp} \end{equation} \]

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
KNAPSACK(v, w, n, W):
  // fill dp table
  for i = 0 to n:
    dp[i][0] = 0
  for c = 0 to W:
    dp[0][c] = 0
  for i = 1 to n:
    for c = 1 to W:
      dp[i][c] = dp[i-1][c]          // exclude item i
      if w[i] ≤ c:
        dp[i][c] = max(dp[i][c], v[i] + dp[i-1][c - w[i]])  // include
  return dp[n][W]

RECONSTRUCT(dp, w, n, W):
  // backtrack to find which items were selected
  items = []
  c = W
  for i = n downto 1:
    if dp[i][c] ≠ dp[i-1][c]:
      items.append(i)
      c = c - w[i]
  return items

docs.title: Space Optimisation
docs.text:
Only the previous row dp[i-1][·] is needed to compute row dp[i][·], so the table can be compressed to a 1D array of length \(W + 1\) by iterating \(c\) from \(W\) downto \(w_i\) (right-to-left):

KNAPSACK-1D(v, w, n, W):
  dp = array of size W+1, initialised to 0
  for i = 1 to n:
    for c = W downto w[i]:           // right-to-left prevents reuse
      dp[c] = max(dp[c], v[i] + dp[c - w[i]])
  return dp[W]

The right-to-left order ensures each item is not counted more than once (i.e. enforces the 0/1 constraint). Left-to-right would give the unbounded knapsack (each item may be selected multiple times).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Aspect Cost Time (DP table) \(O(nW)\) Space (2D table) \(O(nW)\) Space (1D optimised) \(O(W)\) Reconstruction \(O(n)\) (with full table)

\(O(nW)\) is pseudo-polynomial: it is polynomial in \(n\) and the numeric value of \(W\), but exponential in the bit length of the input since \(W\) can be encoded in \(O(\log W)\) bits. No polynomial-time algorithm is known for the exact optimisation problem (NP-hardness follows from reduction from SUBSET-SUM) 12.

docs.title: Fractional Knapsack (Comparison)
docs.text:
In the fractional knapsack problem items can be split: take any fraction \(x_i \in [0, 1]\) of item \(i\). The greedy algorithm (fill items by decreasing \(v_i / w_i\) ratio, taking fractions as needed) is optimal in \(O(n \log n)\) (dominated by sorting). The 0/1 version does not admit a greedy solution because fractional solutions have higher LP relaxation values.

Version Optimal algorithm Complexity Fractional Greedy by ratio \(O(n \log n)\) 0/1 Dynamic programming \(O(nW)\) (pseudo-poly) 0/1 approximation FPTAS \(O(n^2 / \varepsilon)\) for \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approx

docs.title: FPTAS
docs.text: The 0/1 knapsack admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS): scale all values by \(K = \varepsilon v_{\max} / n\) (round down), solve the DP on the scaled values, and map back. The resulting solution has value \(\geq (1 - \varepsilon) \text{OPT}\) and runs in \(O(n^2 / \varepsilon)\) 2.

docs.title: Searching in Data Structures
docs.text: Searching algorithms locate a target element within an explicitly stored, structured collection. Unlike state-space search, the data set is fully materialised: every element already exists in memory and is addressable by index or key.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
Algorithm Paradigm Precondition Worst-case cost Linear Search Brute force None \(O(n)\) Binary Search Divide and conquer Sorted array \(O(\log n)\)

The choice between the two is determined almost entirely by whether the data is sorted and whether the underlying container supports \(O(1)\) random access:

  • Linear search is correct for any sequence regardless of order or container type. It is optimal for unsorted data.
  • Binary search requires a sorted random-access array but reduces the search cost from linear to logarithmic by halving the candidate interval at every step.

More efficient structures — hash tables, balanced BSTs — achieve \(O(1)\) expected or \(O(\log n)\) worst-case lookup but fall under data structure design rather than search algorithm design and are therefore treated separately.

docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text:
Binary search is one of the most fundamental algorithms in computer science: given a sorted array \(A[0..n-1]\) and a target value \(t\), it locates \(t\) — or confirms its absence — in \(O(\log_2 n)\) comparisons by repeatedly halving the candidate range. Knuth 1 traces the idea to the 1940s and notes that, while the principle is elementary, writing a provably correct implementation is surprisingly subtle: the first published bug-free iterative version did not appear until 1962. Cormen et al. 2 classify binary search as the paradigmatic example of the decrease-and-conquer strategy, in which a single comparison eliminates half the remaining search space.

Binary search is often superficially compared to the bisection method, but the two are categorically distinct. Binary search operates on a sorted discrete collection and produces an exact answer (an index or an absence flag); bisection operates on a continuous function and produces an approximation to a root, with a convergence guarantee grounded in the Intermediate Value Theorem. They share a geometric intuition but not a mathematical foundation.

docs.title: Total Order and Sorted Sequences
docs.text:
Binary search requires the array elements to be drawn from a totally ordered set \((S, \leq)\), meaning the relation \(\leq\) is reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, and total (every pair of elements is comparable). For any sorted array, the invariant

\[ \begin{equation} A[i] \leq A[j] \quad \forall\; 0 \leq i < j \leq n-1 \label{sorted_invariant} \end{equation} \]

holds. This invariant is the entire source of binary search's correctness: if \(A[m] < t\) (where \(m = \ell + \lfloor(h - \ell)/2\rfloor\) is the midpoint index, defined precisely in The Algorithm below), then every element at index \(\leq m\) is also \(< t\) by transitivity, allowing the left half to be discarded without inspection.

docs.title: Comparison Complexity Lower Bound
docs.text:
Any algorithm that identifies a target in a sorted sequence using only comparisons must make at least \(\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor\) comparisons in the worst case. This lower bound follows from the information-theoretic argument: each comparison has at most three outcomes (\(<\), \(=\), \(>\)), so a binary decision tree of depth \(d\) can resolve at most \(3 \cdot 2^{d-1}\) outcomes; to distinguish \(n\) positions plus an absence result requires depth at least \(\log_2(n+1)\). Binary search achieves this bound exactly, making it optimal among comparison-based search algorithms 3.

Decision tree argument

A comparison tree models the algorithm as a rooted tree whose internal nodes each represent one comparison \(A[m]\) vs \(t\). Each node has three outgoing edges corresponding to the outcomes \(A[m] < t\), \(A[m] = t\), and \(A[m] > t\). The \(=\) edge leads directly to a leaf (target found); the \(<\) and \(>\) edges recurse to child nodes or to a "not found" leaf. A tree of depth \(d\) has at most \(3 \cdot 2^{d-1}\) leaves (the root contributes 3 branches; each subsequent non-terminal level at most doubles the frontier of live nodes). To distinguish all \(n\) found positions plus one absent outcome requires at least \(n + 1\) reachable leaves, giving \(3 \cdot 2^{d-1} \geq n + 1\) and hence \(d \geq \log_2\!\bigl((n+1)/3\bigr) + 1\). For large \(n\) this simplifies to \(d \geq \log_2(n+1)\). Binary search constructs a tree that reaches exactly this depth, confirming the bound is tight.

docs.title: Iterative Formulation
docs.text:
Maintain two indices \(\ell\) (low) and \(h\) (high) representing the inclusive bounds of the current candidate interval:

\[ \begin{equation} \ell_0 = 0, \qquad h_0 = n - 1 \label{binary_search_init} \end{equation} \] Index notation

Throughout this section a subscript \(k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) denotes the value of a variable at the start of iteration \(k\). Concretely: \(\ell_k\) is the lower bound of the candidate interval entering iteration \(k\); \(h_k\) is the upper bound; \(m_k\) is the midpoint computed during iteration \(k\). After the comparison, whichever of \(\ell\) or \(h\) needs updating is written as \(\ell_{k+1}\) or \(h_{k+1}\) — the value passed into iteration \(k+1\). The algorithm terminates at iteration \(k\) if either \(A[m_k] = t\) (found) or the updated interval satisfies \(\ell_{k+1} > h_{k+1}\) (absent).

At each iteration, compute the midpoint via integer arithmetic to avoid overflow 2:

\[ \begin{equation} m_k = \ell_k + \left\lfloor \frac{h_k - \ell_k}{2} \right\rfloor \label{binary_search_mid} \end{equation} \]

The update rule is a three-way branch:

\[ \begin{equation} (\ell_{k+1},\, h_{k+1}) = \begin{cases} (\ell_k,\; m_k - 1) & \text{if } A[m_k] > t \\ (\text{found at } m_k) & \text{if } A[m_k] = t \\ (m_k + 1,\; h_k) & \text{if } A[m_k] < t \end{cases} \label{binary_search_update} \end{equation} \]

Iteration terminates when a match is found or when \(\ell_k > h_k\), which signals that \(t \notin A\).

docs.title: Worst-Case Comparison Count
docs.text:
Each iteration reduces the interval width \(h_k - \ell_k + 1\) by (at least) half. Starting from width \(n\), the interval reaches width \(\leq 1\) after at most \(\lceil \log_2 n \rceil\) halvings. Knuth 1 gives the exact worst-case count as

\[ \begin{equation} C_{\text{worst}}(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 \label{binary_search_worst} \end{equation} \]

comparisons, and the average count for a successful search (assuming uniform distribution over \(n\) elements) as

\[ \begin{equation} C_{\text{avg}}(n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \lfloor \log_2 j \rfloor + 1 \approx \log_2 n - 1 \label{binary_search_avg} \end{equation} \]

docs.title: Comparison with Linear Search
docs.text:
Linear (sequential) search examines elements one by one, requiring \(O(n)\) comparisons on average and in the worst case. Binary search reduces this to \(O(\log_2 n)\). The practical impact is enormous: for \(n = 10^9\), linear search may require up to \(10^9\) comparisons; binary search requires at most \(30\).

\(n\) Linear (worst) Binary (worst) 16 16 4 1 024 1 024 10 \(10^6\) \(10^6\) 20 \(10^9\) \(10^9\) 30

docs.title: Lower Bound and Upper Bound
docs.text:
Standard binary search finds any occurrence of \(t\). When duplicates are present, two specialised variants are needed 23:

  • Lower bound (lower_bound): returns the index of the first element \(\geq t\). If \(t\) is absent, returns the insertion point that preserves sorted order.
  • Upper bound (upper_bound): returns the index of the first element \(> t\). The range \([\text{lower_bound}(t),\, \text{upper_bound}(t))\) is the interval of all occurrences of \(t\).

Both require only the replacement of the equality check by a one-sided comparison, leaving the \(O(\log n)\) complexity unchanged.

docs.title: Recursive Formulation
docs.text:
Binary search can equally be written recursively:

\[ \text{search}(A,\, t,\, \ell,\, h) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } \ell > h \\ m & \text{if } A[m] = t, \quad m = \ell + \lfloor (h-\ell)/2 \rfloor \\ \text{search}(A,\, t,\, m+1,\, h) & \text{if } A[m] < t \\ \text{search}(A,\, t,\, \ell,\, m-1) & \text{if } A[m] > t \end{cases} \] Scope of \(m\) across the branches

In the piecewise definition above, \(m\) is not independently defined in cases 3 and 4 — it is computed once at the start of each call as \(m = \ell + \lfloor(h - \ell)/2\rfloor\) (stated explicitly as part of case 2). All four cases then refer to this same value: case 1 checks whether the search interval is empty and returns \(-1\) (target absent); case 2 tests \(A[m] = t\) and returns the index \(m\) if so; cases 3 and 4 compare \(A[m]\) with \(t\) and recurse into the appropriate half, passing \(m+1\) or \(m-1\) as the new boundary to exclude the already-tested midpoint. The variable \(m\) is implicitly local to the current call and takes a fresh value in each recursive invocation.

The recurrence for the number of comparisons is \(T(n) = T(n/2) + 1\), \(T(1)=1\), where \(T(n/2)\) reflects the fact that each recursive call searches exactly half the remaining interval. The recurrence solves to \(T(n) = \lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil\) by the Master Theorem — identical to the iterative form.

The recursive version incurs \(O(\log n)\) call-stack frames, giving it \(O(\log n)\) space instead of \(O(1)\) for the iterative version. For very large \(n\) this can matter in practice.

docs.title: Exponential Search
docs.text: When the array size \(n\) is unknown or very large, binary search can be preceded by an exponential phase: examine \(A[1],\, A[2],\, A[4],\, A[8],\, \ldots\) until an element exceeding \(t\) is found, then apply binary search on the identified interval. The total work is \(O(\log i)\) where \(i\) is the position of \(t\) — useful for unbounded arrays or when the target is expected to be near the start 3.

docs.title: Fractional Cascading
docs.text: When the same target must be searched in \(k\) related sorted arrays simultaneously, fractional cascading reduces the total cost from \(O(k \log n)\) to \(O(k + \log n)\) by threading pointers between arrays. This technique is useful in computational geometry and range-tree data structures.

docs.title: Limitations and Challenges
docs.text:
Binary search is only applicable if the following preconditions are met:

  1. Sorted order: The array must satisfy the invariant of Equation \eqref{sorted_invariant}. If the array is unsorted, binary search produces incorrect results without warning. Sorting costs \(O(n \log n)\), which dominates a single search; the algorithm is only worthwhile when many searches are performed on the same sorted data.

  2. Random-access indexing: Binary search computes \(A[m]\) in \(O(1)\) and thus requires a data structure supporting constant-time random access (arrays, vectors). It cannot be applied to linked lists without degrading to \(O(n)\) due to the cost of index traversal.

  3. Static data: Inserting or deleting elements requires re-sorting or using a dynamic structure (balanced BST, skip list), both of which add \(O(\log n)\) overhead per modification. For heavily mutable data, binary search on a raw array is inappropriate.

  4. Exact target required: Binary search finds elements equal to \(t\) exactly. Approximate matching (nearest neighbour, similarity search) requires different methods — k-d trees, LSH, or metric-space indices.

  5. Not for continuous domains: Binary search is not applicable to continuous root-finding problems; that is the domain of bracketing methods such as bisection.

docs.title: Linear Search
docs.text:
Linear search — also called sequential search — is the simplest algorithm for locating a target element in a collection: it inspects each element in turn until a match is found or all elements are exhausted. No preconditions are imposed on the collection; it need not be sorted, contiguous in memory, or even finite in advance. Knuth 1 treats it as the baseline against which every faster search method must justify its additional requirements.

Despite its \(O(n)\) worst-case cost, linear search is often the correct choice in practice: for small or unsorted arrays, for linked lists (which do not support \(O(1)\) random access needed by binary search), and as the inner loop of algorithms that search very short sublists.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given a sequence \(A = \langle a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1} \rangle\) of \(n\) elements drawn from a totally ordered set, and a target value \(t\), find the smallest index \(i\) such that \(a_i = t\), or report that no such index exists.

\[ \begin{equation} \text{result}(A, t) = \begin{cases} \min\{i \in [0, n) : a_i = t\} & \text{if } t \in A \\ \bot & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \label{eq:linear_search_result} \end{equation} \] Variables Symbol Meaning \(A\) The input sequence of length \(n\) \(n\) Number of elements in \(A\) \(a_i\) Element at index \(i\) \(t\) Target value to search for \(\bot\) Sentinel indicating absence

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
The procedure is direct: maintain a cursor \(i\) starting at 0, compare \(a_i\) with \(t\), advance if they differ, and halt when they match or the array ends.

LINEARSEARCH(A, n, t):
  for i = 0 to n - 1:
    if A[i] = t:
      return i
  return ⊥

docs.title: Loop Invariant
docs.text:
At the start of each iteration with cursor value \(i\):

\(t \notin \{a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{i-1}\}\)

That is, the target has not been found in any position before \(i\). On termination either the invariant is broken by a match at position \(i\) (return \(i\)), or \(i\) reaches \(n\) with the invariant still holding, confirming absence (return \(\bot\)).

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
Let \(C(n)\) denote the number of element–target comparisons.

Best case (\(t = a_0\)): the first comparison succeeds.

\[C_{\min} = 1\]

Worst case (\(t \notin A\) or \(t = a_{n-1}\)): every element is inspected.

\[C_{\max} = n\]

Average case (uniform distribution over positions, \(t\) present with probability \(p\)):

The expected number of comparisons when \(t\) is at position \(j\) (uniformly distributed over \(\{0, \ldots, n-1\}\)) is:

\[ \begin{equation} C_{\text{avg}} = p \cdot \frac{n+1}{2} + (1-p) \cdot n \label{eq:linear_avg} \end{equation} \]

When \(t\) is always present (\(p = 1\)): \(C_{\text{avg}} = (n+1)/2\). When \(t\) is never present (\(p = 0\)): \(C_{\text{avg}} = n\).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Case Comparisons Space Best \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) Average \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Worst \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\)

Linear search is in-place (\(O(1)\) extra space) and does not require preprocessing.

docs.title: Optimality
docs.text:
For an unsorted collection with no additional data structure, linear search is information-theoretically optimal: every element must be a candidate until proven otherwise, so any algorithm must in the worst case inspect all \(n\) elements. This follows from an adversary argument: for any deterministic algorithm that halts before inspecting all elements, the adversary can place \(t\) in the last unexamined position.

For a sorted collection, binary search achieves \(O(\log n)\) and is strictly superior for large \(n\) (see Binary Search).

docs.title: Sentinel Search
docs.text:
A sentinel is a copy of \(t\) placed at position \(A[n]\) (a temporary extension of the array) before the scan. This eliminates the bounds check i < n from every iteration, replacing two comparisons per step with one:

SENTINELSEARCH(A, n, t):
  A[n] = t          // write sentinel
  i = 0
  while A[i] ≠ t:
    i = i + 1
  if i < n:
    return i
  return ⊥

The sentinel guarantees the loop terminates without an explicit bounds check. The savings are constant-factor only but matter in tight inner loops on large arrays.

docs.title: Self-Organising Search (Move-to-Front)
docs.text: If elements are searched repeatedly with non-uniform probabilities, moving each found element to the front of the list after each access reduces the expected search length over time. Under the independent reference model, the move-to-front heuristic achieves expected search length that is at most twice optimal for any fixed probability distribution 1.

docs.title: Transposition Search
docs.text: A weaker variant: swap the found element with its predecessor rather than moving it to the front. This adapts more slowly but causes less disruption for distributions where one element does not dominate all searches.

docs.title: Ordered Linear Search
docs.text: When \(A\) is sorted, comparing \(a_i > t\) (rather than just \(a_i \neq t\)) allows early termination on failure: once an element exceeding \(t\) is encountered, all subsequent elements also exceed \(t\), so \(t\) cannot be present. This reduces the average unsuccessful search cost from \(n\) comparisons to \(\approx n/2\).

docs.title: Comparison with Binary Search
docs.text:
Property Linear search Binary search Precondition None Sorted array Data structure Any iterable Random-access array Worst-case cost \(O(n)\) \(O(\log n)\) Best-case cost \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) Preprocessing None Sorting: \(O(n \log n)\) Space \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\)

The crossover point — where the preprocessing cost of sorting amortises over many binary searches — is \(k \approx n \log_2 n / \log_2 n = n\) searches (ignoring constants). For fewer than \(n\) total searches on an unsorted array, linear search is cheaper overall.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Small arrays (\(n \lesssim 8\)): the constant overhead of binary search (index arithmetic, bounds checks) makes linear search faster in practice.
  • Linked structures: traversal is inherently sequential, so \(O(1)\) random access required by binary search is unavailable.
  • Streaming data: elements arrive one at a time with no prior knowledge of the sorted order; search must be done as data is ingested.
  • Last-element searching: variants such as find_last_of in C++ or rfind scan right to left.
  • Inner loop of algorithms: e.g. insertion sort's inner scan to find the insertion position, or linear-time bucket search.

docs.title: Sorting Algorithms
docs.text: Sorting algorithms impose a total order on an unordered sequence. They are among the most studied algorithms in computer science: many other algorithms (binary search, Kruskal's MST, many DP formulations) require sorted input as a precondition, so efficient sorting is foundational rather than incidental.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Algorithm Paradigm Best Average Worst Space Stable Merge Sort Divide and conquer \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n)\) Yes Quick Sort Divide and conquer / Randomised \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n^2)\) \(O(\log n)\) No Heap Sort Heap data structure \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(1)\) No

docs.title: Lower Bound
docs.text: The comparison-based sorting lower bound states that any algorithm that sorts \(n\) elements purely by pairwise comparisons requires at least \(\Omega(n \log n)\) comparisons in the worst case. The argument uses a decision-tree model: a binary tree with \(n!\) leaves (one per permutation) must have height at least \(\log_2(n!) = \Omega(n \log n)\) by Stirling's approximation. Merge sort and heap sort achieve this bound; quick sort achieves it on average. Non-comparison sorts (radix, counting, bucket) bypass the lower bound by exploiting key structure.

docs.title: Heap Sort
docs.text:
Heap sort is an in-place comparison-based sorting algorithm that achieves \(O(n \log n)\) in the worst case without requiring auxiliary memory beyond a fixed number of variables. It was introduced by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 12. The algorithm works in two phases: first it reorganises the input array into a max-heap data structure, then it repeatedly extracts the maximum element and places it at the end of the array, shrinking the heap by one each time.

Heap sort is the only standard algorithm that combines in-place operation with a strict \(O(n \log n)\) worst-case guarantee — a property that neither quick sort (which is \(O(n^2)\) worst case) nor merge sort (which requires \(O(n)\) auxiliary space) achieves simultaneously. However, its poor cache behaviour relative to quick sort means it is rarely the fastest algorithm in practice.

docs.title: Binary Heap (Array Representation)
docs.text:
A max-heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array \(A[0..n-1]\) (using 0-based indexing) satisfying the heap property:

\[ \begin{equation} A[\text{parent}(i)] \geq A[i] \quad \text{for all } i > 0 \label{eq:heap_property} \end{equation} \]

Parent and child indices in 0-based storage:

\[ \text{parent}(i) = \left\lfloor \frac{i - 1}{2} \right\rfloor, \quad \text{left}(i) = 2i + 1, \quad \text{right}(i) = 2i + 2 \] Variables Symbol Meaning \(n\) Number of elements \(A[0..n-1]\) Input array (interpreted as a binary tree) \(\text{heap-size}\) Number of active heap elements (\(\leq n\)) \(i\) Index of a node \(\text{parent}(i)\), \(\text{left}(i)\), \(\text{right}(i)\) Index arithmetic for tree navigation

docs.title: MAX-HEAPIFY Cost
docs.text: Restoring the heap property below node \(i\) in a heap of height \(h\) takes \(O(h)\) comparisons. The height of node \(i\) in a complete binary tree of \(n\) nodes is \(\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor - \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor\), so \(O(\log n)\) in the worst case.

docs.title: BUILD-MAX-HEAP Tight Bound
docs.text:
A naive analysis gives \(O(n \log n)\) for BUILD-MAX-HEAP (calling MAX-HEAPIFY on each of the \(n/2\) interior nodes). The tight bound is \(O(n)\): nodes deep in the tree have small height and cheap heapify calls. Summing:

\[ \begin{equation} \sum_{h=0}^{\lfloor \log n \rfloor} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} \right\rfloor \cdot O(h) = O\!\left(n \sum_{h=0}^{\infty} \frac{h}{2^h}\right) = O(n) \label{eq:build_heap_cost} \end{equation} \]

using \(\sum_{h=0}^{\infty} h/2^h = 2\).

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
MAX-HEAPIFY(A, i, heap-size):
  l = 2i + 1;  r = 2i + 2
  if l < heap-size and A[l] > A[i]: largest = l
  else:                              largest = i
  if r < heap-size and A[r] > A[largest]: largest = r
  if largest ≠ i:
    swap A[i] and A[largest]
    MAX-HEAPIFY(A, largest, heap-size)

BUILD-MAX-HEAP(A, n):
  heap-size = n
  for i = ⌊n/2⌋ - 1 downto 0:   // start from last internal node
    MAX-HEAPIFY(A, i, heap-size)

HEAPSORT(A, n):
  BUILD-MAX-HEAP(A, n)
  for i = n - 1 downto 1:
    swap A[0] and A[i]            // move max to final position
    MAX-HEAPIFY(A, 0, i)          // restore heap on reduced array

docs.title: Why Start BUILD-MAX-HEAP at \(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1\)?
docs.text: Nodes with index \(\geq \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\) are leaves and trivially satisfy the heap property (they have no children). Starting heapification at the last non-leaf node \(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1\) and working upward ensures that when MAX-HEAPIFY is called on a node, both its subtrees are already valid heaps.

docs.title: Correctness: Loop Invariant in HEAPSORT
docs.text:
At the start of each iteration of the for loop with index \(i\):

Sub-array \(A[0..i]\) is a max-heap containing the \(i+1\) smallest elements of the original array; sub-array \(A[i+1..n-1]\) contains the \(n-1-i\) largest elements in sorted order.

Initialisation: after BUILD-MAX-HEAP, \(A[0..n-1]\) is a max-heap (sub-array \(A[i+1..n-1]\) is empty — trivially sorted). Maintenance: swapping \(A[0]\) (max of heap) to \(A[i]\) extends the sorted suffix; MAX-HEAPIFY restores the heap on \(A[0..i-1]\). Termination: when \(i = 0\), the sorted suffix spans the entire array.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Operation Time Space BUILD-MAX-HEAP \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Each EXTRACT-MAX \(O(\log n)\) \(O(1)\) Total HEAPSORT \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(1)\)

All three cases (best, average, worst) are \(O(n \log n)\) because every input leads to exactly \(n - 1\) extract-max operations each costing \(O(\log n)\) 1.

docs.title: In-Place and Not Stable
docs.text: Heap sort sorts in place (\(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond the call stack, which is \(O(\log n)\) due to recursive MAX-HEAPIFY). It is not stable: the relative order of equal elements may change because the swap in the main loop can move elements across the sorted/heap boundary.

docs.title: Cache Behaviour
docs.text: Heap sort is notoriously cache-unfriendly. MAX-HEAPIFY accesses nodes at indices \(i\), \(2i+1\), \(2i+2\), which in a large array are far apart in memory. By contrast, quick sort and merge sort access elements in more localised patterns, leading to better cache line utilisation and explaining why heap sort is slower in practice despite identical asymptotic complexity.

docs.title: d-ary Heap Sort
docs.text: Replacing the binary heap with a \(d\)-ary heap reduces the height of the heap to \(\log_d n\), reducing the number of sift-up operations, but increases the number of comparisons per sift-down (d comparisons per level instead of 2). For \(d = 4\), the total number of comparisons is lower in practice and cache behaviour improves slightly due to better branching factor vs. cache line width trade-off.

docs.title: Min-Heap Variant for Ascending Sort
docs.text: Alternatively, build a min-heap and extract the minimum each time, placing it at the front. Equivalent in complexity; just reverses the implementation.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Priority queues: the heap data structure extracted from heap sort is used standalone as an efficient priority queue in Dijkstra's algorithm, Prim's algorithm, and event-driven simulation.
  • Partial sort / Top-\(k\): to find the top \(k\) elements out of \(n\), build a min-heap of size \(k\) and stream the remaining \(n - k\) elements through it in \(O(n \log k)\) time — far better than full sort when \(k \ll n\).
  • Guaranteed worst-case sort: used as the fallback in introsort (C++ std::sort) to prevent quick sort's \(O(n^2)\) degeneration.

docs.text:

docs.title: Merge Sort
docs.text: Merge sort is the archetypal divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. Given an array of \(n\) elements it recursively splits the array into two halves, sorts each half independently, and then merges the two sorted halves into a single sorted sequence in \(O(n)\) time. The total cost satisfies a recurrence that evaluates to the information-theoretically optimal \(O(n \log n)\). Cormen et al. 1 introduce merge sort as the first major algorithm studied in CLRS precisely because its recurrence, proof of correctness, and stability make it the cleanest illustration of the divide-and-conquer paradigm.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: Given a sequence \(A = \langle a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1} \rangle\) drawn from a totally ordered set, produce a permutation \(A'\) such that \(a'_0 \leq a'_1 \leq \cdots \leq a'_{n-1}\).

docs.title: Recurrence
docs.text:
Splitting an array of size \(n\) into two halves and merging the sorted results gives the recurrence:

\[ \begin{equation} T(n) = 2\,T\!\left(\frac{n}{2}\right) + O(n), \quad T(1) = O(1) \label{eq:mergesort_recurrence} \end{equation} \]

By the Master Theorem with \(a = 2\), \(b = 2\), \(k = 1\) (so \(a = b^k\), case 2):

\[ T(n) = O(n \log n) \]

This holds in the best, average, and worst case — merge sort has no bad inputs.

docs.title: Comparison Lower Bound
docs.text:
Any comparison-based sorting algorithm requires \(\Omega(n \log n)\) comparisons in the worst case. The argument uses a decision-tree model: a binary tree whose leaves represent the \(n!\) possible input permutations must have height \(\geq \log_2(n!) = \Omega(n \log n)\) by Stirling's formula. Merge sort achieves this bound, making it asymptotically optimal among comparison-based sorts 1.

Variables Symbol Meaning \(n\) Number of elements in the array \(A[p..r]\) Sub-array from index \(p\) to index \(r\) (inclusive) \(q = \lfloor (p + r) / 2 \rfloor\) Midpoint index \(T(n)\) Total comparisons / work as a function of \(n\)

docs.title: Top-Down (Recursive)
docs.text:
MERGESORT(A, p, r):
  if p < r:
    q = ⌊(p + r) / 2⌋
    MERGESORT(A, p, q)
    MERGESORT(A, q + 1, r)
    MERGE(A, p, q, r)

MERGE(A, p, q, r):
  // copy left and right halves into temporary arrays L, R
  n₁ = q - p + 1;  n₂ = r - q
  for i = 0 to n₁ - 1: L[i] = A[p + i]
  for j = 0 to n₂ - 1: R[j] = A[q + 1 + j]
  i = 0;  j = 0;  k = p
  while i < n₁ and j < n₂:
    if L[i] ≤ R[j]:  A[k] = L[i];  i++
    else:             A[k] = R[j];  j++
    k++
  // copy any remaining elements
  while i < n₁: A[k++] = L[i++]
  while j < n₂: A[k++] = R[j++]

Initial call: MERGESORT(A, 0, n - 1).

docs.title: Correctness: Loop Invariant in MERGE
docs.text:
At the start of each iteration of the outer while loop in MERGE, with cursor \(k\):

Sub-array \(A[p..k-1]\) contains the \(k - p\) smallest elements of \(L \cup R\), in sorted order.

Initialisation: \(k = p\), the sub-array is empty — trivially holds. Maintenance: each step places min(L[i], R[j]) at \(A[k]\), which is the \((k - p + 1)\)-th smallest element of \(L \cup R\). Termination: when one pointer is exhausted the remaining elements are already in sorted order and are copied directly.

docs.title: Bottom-Up (Iterative) Variant
docs.text: The recursion can be eliminated by merging sub-arrays of increasing size \(w = 1, 2, 4, \ldots\) in a single left-to-right pass per doubling. This avoids function call overhead and is preferred in production implementations.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Case Time Space Best \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n)\) Average \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n)\) Worst \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n)\)

The \(O(n)\) auxiliary space is used for the temporary arrays in MERGE. In-place merge sort variants exist but either sacrifice the \(O(n \log n)\) time or require complex pointer manipulation 1.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text: Merge sort is stable: equal elements appear in the original relative order in the sorted output. This follows directly from the ≤ comparison in MERGE: when L[i] = R[j], the left element is chosen first, preserving relative order. Stability is critical when sorting compound records (e.g. sorting first by last name, then by first name using two stable passes is equivalent to a single two-key sort).

docs.title: External Sorting
docs.text: Merge sort is the basis of external sorting — sorting data sets larger than main memory. The array is divided into runs small enough to fit in RAM, each run is sorted in memory, and runs are then merged from disk. The number of passes over the data is \(O(\log_k n)\) where \(k\) is the number of simultaneous merge streams, and is determined by available memory 21.

docs.title: Comparison with Other Sorts
docs.text:
Property Merge Sort Quick Sort Heap Sort Worst-case time \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n^2)\) \(O(n \log n)\) Average-case time \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) Space \(O(n)\) \(O(\log n)\) \(O(1)\) Stable Yes No (typical) No Cache behaviour Good (sequential) Excellent Poor Preferred when Stability needed, external sort General-purpose in-memory In-place strict \(O(n \log n)\)

docs.title: Quick Sort
docs.text: Quick sort is the most widely used general-purpose in-memory sorting algorithm. Introduced by C. A. R. Hoare in 1959-1962 12, it selects a pivot element, partitions the array into elements smaller than the pivot and elements larger, and recursively sorts each partition. Its expected \(O(n \log n)\) cost combined with exceptional cache performance makes it roughly two to three times faster than merge sort in practice on modern hardware, despite an identical asymptotic average complexity.

docs.title: Partitioning Invariant
docs.text:
After a Lomuto partition step on sub-array \(A[p..r]\) with pivot \(x = A[r]\):

\[ \begin{equation} A[p..q-1] \leq A[q] = x \leq A[q+1..r] \label{eq:qs_partition} \end{equation} \]

Every element left of index \(q\) is \(\leq x\); every element right is \(\geq x\).

docs.title: Recurrence and Expected Complexity
docs.text:
Let pivot rank \(k\) be uniform over \(\{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}\). Then:

\[ T(n) = T(k) + T(n - 1 - k) + \Theta(n) \]

Taking expectation over \(k\):

\[ \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}[T(n)] = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \bigl(\mathbb{E}[T(k)] + \mathbb{E}[T(n-1-k)]\bigr) + \Theta(n) \label{eq:qs_recurrence} \end{equation} \]

Solving via substitution with \(\mathbb{E}[T(n)] \leq cn\ln n\):

\[\mathbb{E}[T(n)] = O(n \log n)\]

The constant is approximately \(2n \ln n \approx 1.386\, n \log_2 n\) comparisons, which is larger than merge sort's \((n \log_2 n)\) theoretical minimum but offset by far lower memory traffic 21.

docs.title: Worst Case
docs.text:
When the pivot is always the minimum or maximum (e.g. sorted or reverse-sorted input with a naive pivot selection), all \(n - 1\) elements fall on one side:

\[T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(n) \implies T(n) = O(n^2)\]

Randomised pivot selection makes this event have probability \(1/n!\) for any fixed input.

Variables Symbol Meaning \(A[p..r]\) Sub-array being sorted \(x\) Pivot element \(q\) Final pivot index after partition \(k\) Rank of the pivot (number of elements smaller) \(T(n)\) Number of comparisons as a function of \(n\)

docs.title: Lomuto Partition
docs.text:
PARTITION(A, p, r):
  x = A[r]          // pivot is last element
  i = p - 1
  for j = p to r - 1:
    if A[j] ≤ x:
      i = i + 1
      swap A[i] and A[j]
  swap A[i + 1] and A[r]
  return i + 1       // final pivot index q

QUICKSORT(A, p, r):
  if p < r:
    q = PARTITION(A, p, r)
    QUICKSORT(A, p, q - 1)
    QUICKSORT(A, q + 1, r)

docs.title: Randomised Pivot
docs.text:
RANDOMISED-PARTITION(A, p, r):
  i = RANDOM(p, r)
  swap A[i] and A[r]
  return PARTITION(A, p, r)

Randomly selecting the pivot before calling PARTITION transforms any fixed input pattern into one that behaves like a random permutation, eliminating the \(O(n^2)\) worst case with high probability 2.

docs.title: Hoare Partition (original)
docs.text:
Hoare's original scheme uses two inward-moving pointers and performs fewer swaps on average (one third as many as Lomuto):

HOARE-PARTITION(A, p, r):
  x = A[p]          // pivot is first element
  i = p - 1
  j = r + 1
  while true:
    repeat j = j - 1 until A[j] ≤ x
    repeat i = i + 1 until A[i] ≥ x
    if i < j: swap A[i] and A[j]
    else:     return j
Note on Hoare's pivot index

Hoare's scheme returns \(j\), not the final pivot position. The pivot is not necessarily at \(A[j]\) after partitioning. Recursive calls should therefore be QUICKSORT(A, p, j) and QUICKSORT(A, j+1, r), not QUICKSORT(A, p, j-1).

docs.title: Correctness: Loop Invariant in PARTITION (Lomuto)
docs.text:
At the start of each iteration with index \(j\):

  1. All elements in \(A[p..i]\) satisfy \(A[k] \leq x\).
  2. All elements in \(A[i+1..j-1]\) satisfy \(A[k] > x\).
  3. \(A[r] = x\).

Each iteration either extends region 1 (when \(A[j] \leq x\), swap brings it into \(A[p..i]\)) or extends region 2 (when \(A[j] > x\), \(j\) advances).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Case Time Space (stack) Best \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(\log n)\) Average \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(\log n)\) Worst \(O(n^2)\) \(O(n)\)

The \(O(\log n)\) stack depth comes from always recursing on the shorter partition first; if the longer partition is recursed first the stack depth can reach \(O(n)\).

docs.title: Three-Way Partition (Dutch National Flag)
docs.text:
When there are many equal keys, the standard partition degenerates: all equal elements repeatedly end up in the same partition, degrading to \(O(n^2)\) on arrays with few distinct values. Dijkstra's Dutch National Flag partition splits the array into three regions:

\[A[p..lt-1] < x \leq A[lt..gt] = x \leq A[gt+1..r] > x\]

Elements equal to the pivot are placed in the middle region and are already sorted; only the strictly smaller and strictly larger regions are recursed on. This achieves \(O(n)\) on arrays with \(O(1)\) distinct keys 1.

docs.title: Introsort
docs.text: The C++ standard library std::sort uses introsort: quick sort until the recursion depth exceeds \(2 \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor\), then switch to heap sort. This ensures \(O(n \log n)\) worst case while retaining quick sort's cache-friendly average-case performance.

docs.title: Median-of-Three Pivot
docs.text: Choose the pivot as the median of \(A[p]\), \(A[\lfloor (p+r)/2 \rfloor]\), and \(A[r]\). Eliminates worst-case behaviour on sorted and reverse-sorted input, at the cost of two extra comparisons per call.

docs.title: State-Space Search
docs.text:
State-space search algorithms navigate an implicitly defined graph whose nodes are states — configurations of a problem — and whose edges are actions or transitions. Unlike data-structure searching, the graph is not stored in memory; it is generated on the fly as the algorithm expands nodes.

This framework, developed in artificial intelligence 12, unifies a broad class of problems: puzzles, planning, routing, and game playing can all be cast as finding a path from an initial state \(s_0\) to a goal state \(g\) in a state-space graph.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Algorithm Searches by Completeness Optimal? Paradigm Uniform-Cost Search Path cost \(g(n)\) Yes Yes Uninformed Greedy Best-First Heuristic \(h(n)\) Yes (finite) No Informed / Greedy A* Search \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\) Yes Yes (admissible \(h\)) Informed / Heuristic Iterative Deepening Depth limit (DFS) Yes Yes (unit cost) Uninformed

docs.title: Uninformed vs. Informed Search
docs.text:
Uninformed (blind) algorithms explore the state space using only structural information: which states exist, which transitions are available, and what the transition costs are. They make no assumptions about which part of the space is likely to contain the goal.

Informed algorithms additionally use a heuristic function \(h(n)\), a domain-specific estimate of the cost from state \(n\) to the nearest goal. A good heuristic dramatically reduces the number of states explored; a perfect heuristic reduces exploration to the optimal path alone.

Variables Symbol Meaning \(s_0\) Initial state \(g\) Goal state or goal test \(g(n)\) Exact cost of the path from \(s_0\) to \(n\) found so far \(h(n)\) Heuristic estimate of cost from \(n\) to the nearest goal \(h^*(n)\) True (optimal) cost from \(n\) to the nearest goal \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\) Evaluation function used by A* \(b\) Branching factor — maximum number of successors of any node \(d\) Depth of the shallowest goal node

docs.title: A* Search Method
docs.text: The A* search algorithm was introduced in 1968 by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael at Stanford Research Institute 1. It stands as one of the most influential algorithms in artificial intelligence, combining the completeness of uninformed search with the efficiency of heuristic guidance. A* is the foundation for a vast family of pathfinding methods used in robotics, navigation, game AI, and combinatorial optimisation.

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
A* is a best-first search algorithm that operates on a graph \(G = (V, E)\) starting from a node \(s\) and expanding nodes in an order determined by an evaluation function. It does not explicitly "search for the minimum-cost path" in the sense of enumerating and comparing all paths. Instead, it follows a principled expansion strategy: at each step it selects from an open list the node \(n\) that minimises:

\[ \begin{equation} f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \label{eq:astar_eval} \end{equation} \]

Here \(g(n)\) is the exact cost of the cheapest path found so far from the start node \(s\) to node \(n\), and \(h(n)\) is a heuristic function estimating the cost of the cheapest path from \(n\) to the goal. The function \(f(n)\) therefore estimates the total cost of a solution that passes through \(n\). This interplay between known cost and estimated future cost is what distinguishes A* from pure breadth-first or depth-first expansion, and equally from greedy best-first search, which considers only \(h(n)\) and may follow misleading short-term shortcuts.

The key theoretical result, and the central contribution of Hart, et.al. in 1968 paper 1, is that under a specific condition on the heuristic (admissibility, defined below), the first path the algorithm finds to the goal is provably optimal. Optimality is therefore a consequence of the algorithm's behaviour, not an explicit objective encoded in its mechanics.

docs.title: Admissibility and Optimality
docs.text:
A heuristic \(h(n)\) is called admissible if it never overestimates the true cost \(h^*(n)\) to the goal:

\[ \begin{equation} h(n) \leq h^*(n) \quad \forall\, n \in V \label{eq:admissibility} \end{equation} \]

When the heuristic is admissible, A is guaranteed to find an optimal solution the first time it expands the goal node. This result was proved formally in the original paper by Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael 1 and is the central theoretical guarantee that made A so attractive to the AI community. A stronger property, consistency (also called monotonicity), requires that for every edge \((n, n')\) with cost \(c(n, n')\):

\[ \begin{equation} h(n) \leq c(n, n') + h(n') \label{eq:consistency} \end{equation} \]

A consistent heuristic is always admissible, and when consistency holds the \(f\)-values along any path are non-decreasing, which allows A* to avoid re-expanding nodes it has already closed—making the algorithm more efficient in practice. Russell and Norvig provide a thorough treatment of both conditions and their consequences 2.

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
A maintains two sets. The open list (typically a min-priority queue ordered by \(f\)) holds nodes that have been generated but not yet expanded. The closed list* (or visited set) holds nodes that have already been expanded.

The algorithm begins by placing \(s\) in the open list with \(g(s) = 0\). At each iteration it extracts the node \(n\) with the smallest \(f(n)\). If \(n\) is the goal, the path is reconstructed by tracing back through parent pointers and the procedure terminates. Otherwise \(n\) is moved to the closed list and each of its successors \(n'\) is evaluated. If \(n'\) has not been seen before, or if the path through \(n\) offers a lower \(g\)-value than any previously recorded path, \(n'\) is inserted or updated in the open list with:

\[ \begin{equation} g(n') = g(n) + c(n, n'), \qquad f(n') = g(n') + h(n') \label{eq:astar_update} \end{equation} \]

The algorithm is both complete (it will always find a solution if one exists on a finite graph) and, under admissibility, optimally efficient: no algorithm with the same heuristic information can expand fewer nodes while guaranteeing optimality 3.

docs.title: Heuristic Design
docs.text:
The practical performance of A depends critically on the quality of \(h(n)\). A heuristic that is well-informed—meaning \(h(n)\) is close to \(h^*(n)\)—leads to far fewer node expansions than a weak or uninformative one. A classic example is the Manhattan distance* heuristic used in grid-based pathfinding, which counts the minimum number of horizontal and vertical steps between two cells and is admissible whenever diagonal moves are forbidden. For the Euclidean plane, the straight-line distance to the goal is a natural admissible heuristic.

Judea Pearl thoroughly analyses the relationship between heuristic accuracy and search efficiency in his monograph on heuristic search 3, showing that the expected number of node expansions grows polynomially with problem size when a tight heuristic is available, compared to exponential growth with an uninformative one. In practice, designing a good heuristic often requires deep domain knowledge, and there is no universal recipe for obtaining one.

docs.title: Variants and Extensions
docs.text:
Several important variants of A address its limitations. IDA* (Iterative Deepening A), introduced by Korf, eliminates the open list by performing iterative deepening with the \(f\)-cost as the threshold, drastically reducing memory requirements while preserving optimality. SMA* (Simplified Memory-Bounded A) discards the least promising frontier nodes whenever memory is exhausted, retaining enough information to regenerate them if needed. Weighted A** relaxes the optimality requirement by using:

\[ \begin{equation} f(n) = g(n) + w \cdot h(n), \quad w > 1 \label{eq:weighted_astar} \end{equation} \]

trading solution quality (the returned path costs at most \(w \cdot f^*\)) for substantially faster search. These extensions, along with their formal analyses, are discussed in detail by Russell and Norvig 2.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: In the worst case, A expands all nodes \(n\) with \(f(n) < f^*\), where \(f^*\) is the optimal solution cost. The time complexity is therefore exponential in the depth of the solution, identical to that of uninformed search in the worst case. However, with a near-perfect heuristic the number of expanded nodes approaches the length of the optimal path itself, making A effectively polynomial in practice. The space complexity is \(O(b^d)\), where \(b\) is the branching factor and \(d\) is the depth of the shallowest optimal solution, since all generated nodes must be retained in memory.

docs.title: Applications and Relevance
docs.text: Since its introduction, A has become the reference algorithm for single-source shortest-path problems in AI. It underlies route-planning systems in mapping services such as GPS navigation, robotic motion planning where a robot must move around obstacles, video game pathfinding where hundreds of agents may search simultaneously, and natural language parsing where the search space is a lattice of partial analyses. Nilsson 4 provided early context for A's role within the broader landscape of problem-solving methods in AI, helping establish it as a go-to technique for graph search.

docs.title: Limitations and Challenges
docs.text: Despite its strengths, A faces meaningful challenges in practice. Its memory requirements can become prohibitive in large state spaces, since all frontier nodes must be stored simultaneously in the open list. Designing an effective admissible heuristic is non-trivial and highly domain-dependent; a poor heuristic degrades performance toward that of Dijkstra's algorithm or worse. A is also sensitive to the representation of the problem: the same search problem formulated with a finer or differently structured state space may require orders of magnitude more computation. Finally, in dynamic environments where edge costs change while the algorithm runs, A must be restarted or replaced with incremental variants such as D or D* Lite, which update the search tree efficiently as new information arrives.

docs.title: Interactive Demonstration
docs.text:
The animation below runs A step by step on a small grid. Each cell in the open list shows its current \(f\), \(g\), and \(h\) values. The Manhattan distance is used as the heuristic. Use Step to advance one expansion at a time, or Play* to run automatically.

The numbers along the top and left edges are the column and row indices of each cell. The start node S sits at (row 1, col 1) and the goal G at (row 8, col 12). Because no moves have been made yet, \(g(s)=0\), so the initial \(f\)-value is driven entirely by the heuristic:

\[h(s) = |1-8| + |1-12| = 7 + 11 = 18\]

This is the Manhattan distance — the minimum number of horizontal and vertical steps needed to reach the goal on an obstacle-free grid.

docs.title: Best-First Search
docs.text:
Best-first search is the foundational strategy underlying all informed graph search algorithms in artificial intelligence. Unlike uninformed methods (breadth-first, depth-first, Dijkstra), which explore the graph without any knowledge about the goal's location, best-first search uses a heuristic evaluation function to prioritise nodes that appear more promising, steering the search toward the goal and reducing wasted exploration. Nilsson 1 introduced the central framework and Russell and Norvig 2 give its modern treatment as the template from which A*, beam search, and many planning algorithms are derived.

The term best-first does not refer to a single algorithm but to a class of algorithms: any method that maintains a priority queue of candidate nodes and always expands the one ranked highest by some evaluation criterion is a best-first search. The classic and simplest member of this class is greedy best-first search, which evaluates nodes using only the heuristic estimate \(h(n)\) of distance to the goal, ignoring the cost already paid to reach \(n\). Its more powerful relative, A* (see A* Search), adds the past cost to obtain the exact evaluation function \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\), recovering optimality guarantees that greedy best-first search sacrifices.

docs.title: Graph and Notation
docs.text:
The search operates on a directed graph \(G = (V, E)\) where \(V\) is the set of nodes (states) and \(E \subseteq V \times V\) is the set of directed edges (transitions). Each edge \((n, n')\) carries a non-negative cost \(c(n, n') \geq 0\).

Variable glossary Symbol Meaning \(G = (V, E)\) Search graph: nodes \(V\) (states), edges \(E\) (transitions) \(s \in V\) Start node \(g \in V\) Goal node \(n, n' \in V\) Generic nodes; \(n'\) is a successor of \(n\) \(c(n, n')\) Edge cost from \(n\) to \(n'\) \(\pi(s, n)\) A path from \(s\) to \(n\) (sequence of nodes) \(h(n)\) Heuristic: estimated cost from \(n\) to \(g\) \(h^*(n)\) True optimal cost from \(n\) to \(g\) \(b\) Branching factor: maximum number of successors of any node \(d\) Depth of the shallowest goal node reachable from \(s\)

docs.title: The Evaluation Function
docs.text:
Greedy best-first search assigns each node \(n\) a priority score equal to the heuristic estimate alone:

\[ \begin{equation} f_{\text{greedy}}(n) = h(n) \label{eq:bestfirst_eval} \end{equation} \]

where \(h(n)\) is any function \(V \to [0, \infty)\) that estimates the cost of the cheapest path from \(n\) to the goal \(g\). The open list is a min-priority queue ordered by \(f_{\text{greedy}}\), so the node appearing closest to the goal by the heuristic's measure is always expanded next.

This single-mindedness is both the strength and the weakness of greedy best-first. When \(h(n)\) is accurate, the algorithm cuts a near-straight path to the goal. When \(h(n)\) is misleading — underestimating the difficulty of a region — the algorithm confidently walks into a dead end and must backtrack, potentially exploring far more nodes than an uninformed search would.

docs.title: Heuristic Design
docs.text:
The practical behaviour of any best-first algorithm is entirely determined by \(h(n)\). Pearl 3 systematically analyses the relationship between heuristic accuracy and search cost, showing that the expected number of node expansions grows polynomially with problem size when \(h(n) \approx h^*(n)\), but exponentially when \(h\) is weak. Three properties of heuristics are particularly important:

Admissibility. A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates:

\[ \begin{equation} h(n) \leq h^*(n) \quad \forall\, n \in V \label{eq:admissibility} \end{equation} \]

Admissibility is not required for greedy best-first search — only for A* to guarantee optimality — but an inadmissible heuristic can cause greedy best-first to follow even more misleading paths.

Dominance. Heuristic \(h_2\) dominates \(h_1\) if \(h_2(n) \geq h_1(n)\) for all \(n\) while both remain admissible. A dominant heuristic is always preferable: it expands strictly fewer nodes without losing optimality 2.

Common examples. For grid pathfinding with only horizontal and vertical moves, the Manhattan distance

\[ \begin{equation} h_{\text{Manhattan}}(n) = |r_n - r_g| + |c_n - c_g| \label{eq:manhattan} \end{equation} \]

is admissible (it equals the true cost when the path is unobstructed) and dominates the trivial zero heuristic. Here \(r_n, c_n\) are the row and column of node \(n\), and \(r_g, c_g\) those of the goal. For free Euclidean movement the straight-line distance \(h_{\text{Euclidean}}(n) = \sqrt{(r_n - r_g)^2 + (c_n - c_g)^2}\) is a natural admissible heuristic.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
Greedy best-first search maintains:

  • Open list \(\mathcal{O}\): a min-priority queue of nodes seen but not yet expanded, keyed by \(h(n)\).
  • Closed list \(\mathcal{C}\): the set of nodes already expanded (to prevent re-expansion).
  • Parent map \(\pi\): records the predecessor of each node on the path currently known to reach it, enabling path reconstruction.

Starting with \(\mathcal{O} = \{s\}\) and \(\mathcal{C} = \emptyset\), the algorithm iterates:

  1. If \(\mathcal{O}\) is empty, terminate — no path exists.
  2. Remove \(n = \arg\min_{v \in \mathcal{O}}\, h(v)\) from \(\mathcal{O}\).
  3. If \(n = g\), reconstruct the path via \(\pi\) and return it.
  4. Add \(n\) to \(\mathcal{C}\).
  5. For each successor \(n'\) of \(n\) with edge \((n, n') \in E\):
    • If \(n' \in \mathcal{C}\), skip (already expanded).
    • If \(n' \notin \mathcal{O}\), insert \(n'\) into \(\mathcal{O}\) and record \(\pi(n') = n\).
  6. Go to step 1.

docs.title: Loop Invariant
docs.text:
At the start of each iteration the following invariant holds:

Every node \(n \in \mathcal{O}\) has been reachable from \(s\) via at least one path, and every node \(n \in \mathcal{C}\) has already been expanded — all its successors have been generated and inserted into \(\mathcal{O}\) if not previously seen.

This invariant ensures that if a path to the goal exists and all reachable nodes are eventually inserted into \(\mathcal{O}\), the goal will eventually be removed and returned. However, the path returned is not guaranteed to be the cheapest one, because the algorithm may have reached the goal via a high-cost route that happened to pass through nodes with low \(h\)-values.

docs.title: Comparison with A*
docs.text:
The only algorithmic difference between greedy best-first and A* is the priority key:

Algorithm Priority key Optimal? Complete? Greedy best-first \(h(n)\) No Yes (finite graphs with dup. detection) A* \(g(n) + h(n)\) Yes (admissible \(h\)) Yes Dijkstra \(g(n)\) Yes Yes Depth-first \(-\text{depth}(n)\) No No (infinite graphs)

Dropping \(g(n)\) from the priority makes greedy best-first faster in practice — it expands far fewer nodes when the heuristic is good — at the cost of the optimality guarantee. When reaching the goal quickly matters more than finding the cheapest path (real-time games, approximate planning), greedy best-first is often the right trade-off 2.

docs.title: Completeness
docs.text:
Greedy best-first search is complete on finite graphs when a visited set (the closed list \(\mathcal{C}\)) is maintained: every node can be reached in finitely many expansions, and duplicate detection ensures no node is expanded twice, so the algorithm must terminate.

On infinite graphs or graphs without duplicate detection it may cycle indefinitely. In the pathological case where a low-\(h\) region forms a sink — nodes that look close to the goal but are surrounded by obstacles — the algorithm will fill \(\mathcal{O}\) with nodes in that region and never escape without explicit backtracking.

docs.title: Optimality: Why It Fails
docs.text:
Consider the following scenario: the goal \(g\) is reachable by two paths. Path A has total cost 5 but passes through nodes with large \(h\)-values. Path B has total cost 20 but its intermediate nodes all have small \(h\)-values (they are physically close to the goal but separated from it by an obstacle). Greedy best-first will always prefer nodes on Path B, and will find the goal via the expensive route. Neither tie-breaking nor admissibility of \(h\) prevents this: the algorithm has no information about costs already paid.

Formally, optimality requires that the first time the goal is extracted from the open list its associated path is cheapest. In A* this is guaranteed by the monotone non-decreasing property of \(f = g + h\) along any path under a consistent heuristic. In greedy best-first, \(f = h\) has no such property and the ordering of the open list can be completely unrelated to path cost 3.

docs.title: Variants and Extensions
docs.text:
Beam search is best-first with a fixed-width open list: at each step only the \(W\) most promising nodes are retained, and the rest are discarded, bounding memory to \(O(W \cdot b)\). This trades completeness and optimality for speed and memory efficiency, and is widely used in machine translation and speech recognition.

A* (see A* Search) recovers optimality by replacing \(h(n)\) with \(g(n) + h(n)\), and additionally proves that with an admissible heuristic no other algorithm exploring the same nodes can do better 4.

Weighted A* interpolates between greedy best-first and A by using \(f(n) = g(n) + w \cdot h(n)\) for \(w \geq 1\). At \(w = 1\) this is standard A; as \(w \to \infty\) it approaches greedy best-first. The returned path costs at most \(w \cdot f^*\), where \(f^*\) is the optimal solution cost 2.

Bidirectional best-first search runs two simultaneous greedy searches — one forward from \(s\), one backward from \(g\) — and halts when the two frontiers meet, potentially halving the depth explored.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
In the worst case, greedy best-first search with branching factor \(b\) and maximum depth \(m\) generates at most \(O(b^m)\) nodes in both time and space. The open list holds all generated but unexpanded nodes simultaneously, so memory is the binding constraint in large state spaces.

When the heuristic is well-informed, the effective branching factor \(b^* < b\) is substantially smaller. Pearl 3 shows that for a heuristic with relative error \(\epsilon\) (i.e. \(h(n) \geq (1-\epsilon) h^*(n)\)), the expected number of expansions grows as \(O(n^\epsilon)\) — polynomial rather than exponential in the path length.

docs.title: Limitations and Challenges
docs.text:
Optimality is not guaranteed. Because the cost already paid (\(g(n)\)) is ignored, the algorithm may reach the goal via a long, expensive detour. In applications where solution cost matters — route planning, shortest-path problems — greedy best-first is insufficient on its own.

Heuristic design is domain-specific and non-trivial. A heuristic that is too weak (e.g., constant \(h(n) = 0\)) degrades greedy best-first to breadth-first search; one that severely overestimates will cause the algorithm to behave erratically, expanding nodes that are actually far from the goal. There is no general-purpose recipe for constructing tight heuristics 3.

Memory can become a bottleneck. In large state spaces the open list may grow to hold millions of nodes. Beam search variants cap memory but sacrifice completeness and optimality. A* with consistent heuristics spends memory more efficiently by never re-expanding closed nodes, but still requires \(O(b^d)\) space.

Cycles and repeated states. Without a closed list, greedy best-first in cyclic graphs will loop indefinitely. Maintaining the closed list adds \(O(|V|)\) memory and \(O(\log |V|)\) per-expansion overhead for lookup.
